subtopic: PRELIMINARY ANNOUNCEMENT

speakeroldname: Mr. J. H. Dickey (Parliamentary Assistant, for the Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PRELIMINARY ANNOUNCEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will have noticed by the newspapers that the negotiations at the United Nations wheat conference are drawing to a conclusion. Although some details remain to be determined, it is evident that an international wheat agreement will emerge from the conference.
The minimum price will be $1.50 per bushel and the maximum price $2.00 per bushel, for No. 1 northern in store Fort William/Port Arthur. This represents a nominal reduction from the present range of $1.55-$2.05.
The quantities have yet to be finally determined. There will be a proportionate reduction in the shares of all the major exporting countries, members of the present agreement, that is, the United States, Canada and Australia. It is expected that the Canadian quantity will be reduced from about 150 million bushels to about 100 million bushels.
At the opening of the second session of the conference and before there had been any discussion of prices, the United Kingdom stated that it did not intend to be a member of an international wheat agreement along the present lines and withdrew from the prices and quantities negotiations. All other importing countries, members of the present agreement, continued to participate and are expected to sign. All the major wheat exporting countries, Argentina included, participated in the negotiations and are also expected to sign.
Because of the relatively small quantities, the new international wheat agreement will
not be as effective as the Canadian government had hoped it would be in stabilizing prices and markets. The farm advisers to the Canadian delegation, representing the six major farm organizations of the prairie provinces, agreed with the government, however, that notwithstanding inadequate quantities Canada should continue to participate provided there was no substantial reduction in maximum and minimum prices from those included in the present agreement.
The agreement requires to be ratified by the participants and will come into full effect when ratified by countries representing two-thirds of the quantities. Any country will have rights to withdraw if the membership and the quantities in the agreement as ratified are not satisfactory to it.
A full statement will be made by the secretariat at the conclusion of the conference. Arrangements will be made to have that statement tabled when it is received.

Mr. Speaker, on Friday the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) asked me a question concerning an ore ship that had sunk in the St. Clair river.
I am now informed that on Thursday night, April 19, the S.S. A. M. Byers and the S.S. E. M. Ford were in collision in the St. Clair river about a mile below Russell island.
The S.S. A. M. Byers sank in about 17 minutes in a position almost parallel to the centre line of the channel, which at that point is approximately 800 feet wide, and the wreck lies astride the international boundary line. The United States coastguard took charge and stopped traffic until a survey had been made by the United States corps of engineers and traffic was resumed at two a.m. on Saturday.
I am given to understand, although our report has not been confirmed, that traffic is moving through in single file. I might add that I have had a more recent report to the effect that traffic in both directions was resumed over the week end. Salvage equipment is on the site, preparatory to lightering the Byers' cargo and raising the vessel.
Both vessels are on United States registry and there were no Canadian pilots on board. The responsibility for the investigation into the collision will rest with the United States coastguard.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, April 19, consideration in committee of Bill No. 214, to amend the Trans-Canada Highway Act- Mr. Winters-Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
On clause 2-Limitations.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COST OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, after checking Hansard for Thursday I rise to correct a wrong impression created by the figures given by the minister in connection with the distances involved in the Big Bend, Rogers pass and Jumbo pass routes. I am quite sure that the figures were given quite unintentionally in that form but they are apt to cause a false impression in the minds of hon. members and people throughout the country. The minister gave the length of the Big Bend route as 196 miles from Golden to Revelstoke, the Rogers pass route as 88 miles from Golden to Revelstoke, and the Jumbo pass route as 234 miles. However, he did not mention the fact that this is the distance between Mount Eisenhower and Revelstoke, which makes all the difference. A fair comparison would be to give the distances for all routes between Mount Eisenhower and Revelstoke, which would be as follows:
Big Bend	
270	milesRogers pass	
168	milesJumbo pass	
234	miles
Those figures give an entirely different picture so far as distances are concerned. On reading Hansard further I noticed some rather confusing remarks which had been made by one or two members. I wish to re-emphasize the fact that we are not suggesting this route or that route; we are simply asking that there be a proper and adequate survey of all routes before a final decision is made. So far as the Jumbo pass route is concerned, all that we have to date is a walking reconnaissance undertaken by an engineer of the provincial government. On the basis of that walking reconnaissance he made a preliminary report to the minister of highways in British Columbia.


I am rising again on this question because it is an important matter to the people of southeastern British Columbia. They are very concerned about it because they believe that no final decision should be made until there is a proper survey of all routes. You might say that the request that has come from all the chambers of commerce and boards of trade and any number of farmers' institutes and other organizations was reaffirmed on April 14. Did the hon. member for New Westminster wish to make a comment?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COST OF HIGHWAY
speechtext: I just wanted to know whether each individual had written to you.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COST OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
A good number have written to me, but I am representing the views of my constituency and, in this case, the majority of all members of all parties. It is not a partisan matter; it is a district matter; and there are no party politics connected with it. Anyway, these requests that have come during the past two or three years by members or organizations were reaffirmed on April 14 at the annual convention of the associated boards of trade of southeastern British Columbia, held at Invermere. There again they passed a resolution urging a thorough survey of this route before any final decision is made and, I understand, they communicated their wishes again to the provincial government and possibly to our minister in Ottawa.
I feel that many members of the house are misinformed on this question and I feel to some extent the minister has not all the facts. I do not get up here and just talk eyewash, as some people to my left do; I am talking about what I know of the wishes of the people I represent. In order to place the facts before the house, and for the sake of the record, I am going to read briefly two or three paragraphs of a brief prepared by Mr. Boyd C. Affleck, a very prominent engineer in Nelson, who has had long and successful experience in the construction of highways, irrigation systems, industrial plants and things of that sort, and also a lengthy and successful career as a British Columbia land surveyor.
I might point out that this gentleman is taking a thoroughly objective point of view. He is a most ardent supporter of the Social Credit government of British Columbia and he is viewing this question as a good citizen and an engineer with long experience in the district and with some knowledge of what he is talking about. I shall quote briefly from his brief in order to get the record straight, as there is a good deal of misunderstanding and confusion. This is what he has to say in concluding his brief, in connection

with this subject, after making a reconnaissance survey over this route:
Some cost estimates have been made by government highway engineers, both dominion and provincial and will be quoted, but the writer is not able to reconcile them, or to determine what items each estimate includes or excludes, or whether they include or exclude the same items. They are, however, interesting.
A federal government engineer has estimated the cost of rebuilding the Big Bend route to trans-Canada standards at $50,916,000. A provincial government engineer has estimated the cost of the same work at $27,300,000. It does not appear that either has included the cost of completing the Kicking Horse section, from Stephen to Donald, which may roughly be guessed at $10 million more. Taking the mean of the two estimates and adding the Kicking Horse estimate, gives the figures of $49,108,000 for the possible cost of this route.
For the C.P.R. route, the comparable estimates of the two engineers are $2,148,000 and $22 million in both cases again ignoring the cost of completing the Kicking Horse section. By the same process of reasoning as before, which is about all one can do, the resulting estimate for this route is $35,074,000.
For the Jumbo pass route only the provincial government engineer's estimate is available amounting to $35,875,000. He has estimated on a highway from Golden, instead of from Mount Eisenhower but perhaps there would be no great difference in the cost involved. He estimated the cost of the summit tunnel at Jumbo pass at $10 million, which does not seem to adequately evaluate the recently developed tunnel driving economies of tungsten drills, multiple jumbos, delayed action blasting and power mucking, which have revolutionized tunnelling practice in the last few years and have reduced costs immensely.
The writer is informed by a tunnel expert that under the favourable conditions existing at the site, the probable cost should be less than half that estimate.
The board of trade explorers who traversed the Glacier creek valley on two occasions, both before and after the engineer's reconnaissance together with several old time trappers, differ very sharply with him on his appraisal of its road construction difficulties which are, in their opinion, not serious.
To summarize:
Big Bend route, length 270 miles, estimated cost $40,108,000.
C.P.R. route, length 168 miles, estimated cost $35,074,000.
Jumbo pass route, length 234 miles, estimated cost $35,875,000.
It is apparently believed by provincial and dominion officials that on account of the large sums that have and are being expended in the Kicking Horse canyon, the trans-Canada highway is thereby irrevocably tied down to that route and that any discussion of routes west must use Golden as a key point, rather than Mount Eisenhower.
He goes on to summarize the whole purpose of his brief and representations and says:
The whole purpose of this brief is to urge the citizens of British Columbia and their government to investigate this new concept of the Jumbo pass route with the same thoroughness with which the two other routes have been investigated. It deserves it.
Trans-Canada Highway Act
I mention that, Mr. Chairman, because this gentleman does not speak just for the sake of talking. He is a highly qualified engineer indeed.
I want to mention another matter before I sit down. According to the British Columbia papers Mr. Evan Jones, deputy minister of highways for British Columbia, informed the British Columbia tourist council last fall, I think it was in October, at its annual meeting that Rogers pass definitely would be the future link between Revelstoke and Golden. Here is an interesting thing. Here is the deputy minister of highways of British Columbia making a definite announcement before a British Columbia body as to the route of the trans-Canada highway in that section. Yet the Minister of Public Works for Canada apparently has not been informed of the announcement made by the deputy minister of highways of British Columbia. That seems very strange to me. I should like the minister to inform the house if he has any other correspondence from the minister of highways of British Columbia that would indicate that the prior announcement made by the deputy minister of highways with respect to the route of the trans-Canada highway in British Columbia is correct.
I hope the minister can give us some information in that respect because the matter has us all a bit concerned. To show the interest in the matter, I should like to read an excerpt from an article in the Nelson Daily News of March 12, 1956. The article is headed, "Windermere Board Continues to Press for Jumbo Pass Highway." It reads in part as follows:
Invermere-Windermere district board of trade functions on the theory that "you can't keep a good project down."
That is why I am on my feet again today, Mr. Chairman.
In spite of numerous rebuffs on the proposed Jumbo pass highway, the organization bounces back with renewed enthusiasm and strong faith that given a fair survey the Jumbo pass route would stand on its own merits.
In the same spirit, Mr. Chairman, I again ask the minister to use his good offices to make representations to the minister of highways of British Columbia for a fair and adequate survey of the Jumbo pass route before a final decision is made with respect to this very important matter.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COST OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
I only have
a couple of questions. One of them has to do with the observation made on the last day we discussed the bill by the hon. member for St. Paul's. It has to do with the correct wording of subclause 3 (b) of clause 2. He asked the minister to consider whether the clause might not be amended to read

Trans-Canada Highway Act "the total length" and I think the minister replied that he was satisfied that it meant the total length and that it needed no further amendment. In reading subsection 3 which follows, one finds that it deals with the incorporation into this plan of highways already constructed. It again appears to me that there is some substance in the remarks of the hon. member for St. Paul's, and perhaps the minister might repeat the statement that this does definitely include the total length; that is in subsection 3 (b) whether he has considered the suggestion of the amendment. That is one thing I should like to ask the minister.
Then, I am wondering what reason there is for subsection (4) of section 2 which states:
No contributions or payments shall be made under this act,
(a)	after the 31st day of May, 1961.
This would appear to be some form of limitation, as we know it in the law. I can understand the significance of the clause dealing with the construction time, but is there any particular reason why we should set a time limit on the payment? After all, it may be the federal government's fault that payment is not made upon demand by the provinces, yet this section would appear to be mandatory and there would be no opportunity for the provinces to get payment after that date. If the reason for nonpayment were of their own making I could understand that, but there is the possibility "that there may be some omission on the part of the federal government which would push the provinces past this date. 1 find it difficult to understand why that particular subsection is going in the amended act.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COST OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in answer
to those questions I would say that in subsection 3 (b) the length means the total length. I again checked with the law officers this morning and they assured me that the wording in the bill is all right and conveys the intention we have in mind in that respect.
Subsection 4 (a)-it was considered by the treasury officers that there should be some cut-off date. When the provincial governments met with us it was agreed that the termination date for the work would be December 31, 1960. We all agreed that there should be an adequate period allowed for the provinces to submit their accounts for payment. At that time we suggested the end of the fiscal year, March 31, 1961 and I think the provinces all thought that was all right. But then, when the agreement went out to them in draft form, we exchanged some more views with provincial officials and with our own treasury people and it was agreed that if we allowed an

extra two months they could get their accounts in and we could service them; that was agreed upon.

speechtext:
They are
satisfied?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COST OF HIGHWAY
speechtext: I believe they are satisfied.

clause 3?

speechtext:
When the bill is before the house for second reading it will be appropriate for me to make a more general statement.
In 1954 parliament enacted a new National Housing Act containing many of the features

National Housing Act
of the previous legislation, but making important changes relating to loans for home ownership and rental housing by introducing the insured loan technique. Banks were first introduced into mortgaged lending in Canada through the new act and during the year 1955 they were responsible for half the loans committed under the National Housing Act.
In 1955, 127,000 houses were completed and 135,000 were started. This is an all-time record for house building in Canada. About one-half of this large program was financed under the act.
Since the end of world war II almost one million new houses have been built, largely on the perimeters of our cities. There is now increased public concern for housing conditions in the interior of our cities, and it is with this subject that the proposed legislation mainly deals.
The first item on the resolution deals with the redevelopment of substandard areas in municipalities. It is proposed to amend the act in two ways; first, by widening the scope of the legislation so that the redevelopment of cleared areas may be undertaken by private enterprise as well as by public authorities; and second, by providing a more flexible arrangement for the financial assistance offered to municipalities by the federal government. The basis of federal financial participation will remain the same; that is, up to one-half the net cost of acquiring and clearing the area to be redeveloped.
At present the legislation applies only to an area that is to be used either for a low or moderate cost rental housing project or for any federal, provincial or municipal public purpose. The proposed legislation will remove this restriction so that each area cleared may be redeveloped for the purposes for which it is best suited. These may include the uses that are specified at the present time in the act; or the whole or parts of a cleared site may be sold to private enterprise for residential, commercial or industrial uses. Since the purpose of the act is to provide and improve housing, there will be provision, of course, that the effect of any redevelopment will be to improve housing conditions in the community.
At present the federal government may make a grant to a municipality to assist it in acquiring and clearing an area to be redeveloped. The amount of the grant, as I have indicated, is limited to half the difference between the final cost of acquiring and clearing the area, and its sale price or value when cleared. Under the present statute the federal share was therefore paid only after the operation of acquiring and clearing had been completed. Under the proposed legislation the

federal government will be authorized to contribute to a municipality half of the total cost of acquiring and clearing the area, through contributions made during the process of the acquisition and clearing. When the project is disposed of, the federal government will share with the municipality in what is recovered from the sale or other disposition of the cleared area. These two changes in that part of the act which deals with redevelopment are, I feel, of great importance. The prospect of redeveloping a blighted area into a commercial or perhaps industrial area which may be more appropriate to the district and at the same time more productive of revenues will, I believe, encourage a number of cities to participate in urban redevelopment projects. The prospect of having the federal government share the financial burden virtually from the inception of a redevelopment project should provide an incentive as well.
The home improvement provisions of the act are being amended. The resolution refers to an increase in the amount of loan made by approved lenders that may be guaranteed for home improvement purposes. At the present time the amount which was established in 1948 is $2,500 for improvements to a single dwelling and $1,250 for each additional unit in the building. It is proposed that new provisions will authorize the corporation to guarantee a loan up to $4,000 for the first dwelling unit, and $1,500 for each additional unit, and the maximum period of amortization will be extended.
It is proposed that the aggregate amount of loans that may be guaranteed for home improvement purposes be increased from $125 million to $200 million, in order to look after additional loans which are now being made at the rate of about $30 million per year.
The resolution deals with the aggregate amount of loans made by approved lenders that may be insured by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation under part I of the act. The present limit is $2 billion. The proposal is to increase this to $4 billion. Since the introduction of the insured loan system in the 1954 act, an amount of almost $1 billion had been committed by the end of 1955. At this rate, the present limit of $2 billion would be reached by about the middle of next year.
The resolution calls for the provision of funds for the activities of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation under part V of the act. This part of the act deals with housing research and community planning. It is now provided that funds can be drawn from the consolidated revenue fund up to a limit of $5 million. This limit will be continued

but the new legislation* will provide for expenditures under this part of the act to be brought before parliament periodically.
The resolution also calls for a revote of the $50 million at present provided by the existing legislation for federal-provincial land assembly and housing projects. The proposed amendment will simply bring the method of accounting into line with normal government practice.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTRIBUTIONS TO MUNICIPALITIES, HOME LOANS, HOUSING RESEARCH, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it is fair to say the minister's statement does not enlarge very greatly the information contained in the resolution. He has indicated that his statement was to be confined to those aspects of the bill which are of a money nature and require the introduction and adoption of a prior resolution. I think for that reason, since the bill is to contain obviously other amendments to the National Housing Act, I should reserve until we have the bill any comments which may more properly be made on second reading.
I have only two observations to make in general on the resolution as outlined by the minister. In the first place, the house is being asked to approve a considerable enlargement in the funds appropriated by the act for housing under the various parts of the act. The house has never been penny-pinching in its approach to the housing problem.
As to the other feature of the bill which the minister indicates is designed to add greater flexibility to the provisions of the act for its scheme of dealing with the problem of blighted areas, I am sure that the house will be glad to approve in principle any effort to make these provisions of the bill more flexible and more efficacious for the purpose of clearing blighted areas.
This is the first occasion in the last two years that there has been an opportunity for a discussion of housing. Hon. members will recall the extended debate which we had in March 1954 when the new housing act was introduced and discussed on second reading, and then after it was reviewed in the banking and commerce committee when it came back to the house. This is the first occasion since that time that the house has had an opportunity to discuss housing and to review the results achieved under the new measure which has now been in effect for two years.
I should like to make some passing observations on the developments in this field since the new act came into being. I begin by reference to the retirement of Mr. David Mansur, the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, late in the year
National Housing Act
1954. I think all hon. members of the house would like to acknowledge and pay tribute to the devoted service rendered by Mr. Mansur under the very heavy responsibility that fell on his shoulders in the post-war years as president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
It was the good fortune of many hon. members of this house to come into close contact with Mr. Mansur, not only in relation to housing problems that they sought to discuss with him, but also in two sessions when the standing committee on banking and commerce had Mr. Mansur before it as a witness in reviewing housing administration. It is not unfair to say that Mr. Mansur made a profound impression upon the committee not only by his wide knowledge and his thoroughly co-operative attitude but also his forward-looking views. I am sure that in leaving the presidency of Central Mortgage, and Housing Corporation to follow a private career Mr. Mansur carries with him the gratitude and good will of all hon. members of this house.
The second matter worthy of comment is, of course, the high volume of house construction which the minister has mentioned. In 1955 it reached an all-time high of 127,600 houses. There are perhaps four factors that enter into the high volume of housing construction that are worthy of comment.
The first is the participation by the chartered banks in mortgage financing. They have done so on a very extensive basis. When this matter was before the house two years ago there was still some question in view of its novelty as to how far the banks would participate in the new scheme of insured mortgage loans. Perhaps the views of the bank were adequately summed up by Mr. Atkinson on the occasion of his retirement from the presidency of the Canadian Bankers Association last June when he said, as reported in the press:
"There is no doubt,'' he said, "that financing homes under the National Housing Act now is an accepted and integral part of Canadian banking."
Forty per cent of the total number of housing units approved for loans under the National Housing Act are being financed by the chartered banks. "Bank participation," he said, "is a notable contribution toward easing the housing problem throughout Canada."
The second factor, sir, is an ample supply of mortgage money available for loans on new construction of houses.
The third factor has been a relative stability in building costs. There have been some slight increases but as compared with the previous period it has been a period marked by relative stability.

National Housing Act
The fourth factor arises from the fact that there have been no severe, prolonged or overall shortages of building materials. All these factors have entered into the record rate of house construction in 1955.
There has been one other factor that is not so cheering in its results, and that has been a rapid rise in land costs. It has been particularly marked in the urban areas. In my own city of Toronto it was pointed out by Mr. Bates, the new president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, in his submission to the Gordon royal commission that land values had quadrupled since the war in the areas where housing construction is proceeding most actively at the present time.
Another factor has been the very uneven distribution in housing need and consequently the uneven distribution of the building program to meet it. In this field national averages, after all, are not nearly as significant as they usually are because here we are dealing principally with a need that takes its most acute form in the large urban areas and on their fringes. It is there that the largest increases in population have been occurring.
It remains a fact, as we in this part of the house pointed out two years ago in the debates on the new bill, that the housing problem constitutes a very severe test of the financial strength of municipalities. There is still a lamentable dearth of serviced land, particularly in the areas of greatest need, and this is today the major bottleneck in the path of construction to meet the need.
The municipalities on whom the burden of providing services for land normally falls are literally at the end of their revenue resources. The federal government has within its power the solution of this serious and critical problem, but it continues to withhold that solution. It leaves the responsibility to the provinces, which of course created the municipalities, and at the same time in large measure it continues to absorb their sources of taxation.
I affirm again as on previous occasions that the solution rests within the power of the federal government. The federal government is not coming forward with any solution of this problem, which is not going to be solved without remedial action on the part of the federal authorities. It is to be hoped that this type of action will come soon.
Another feature of developments has been that most of our new housing has been constructed for sale. There is still relatively little construction for renting except in the case of apartment houses, and by and large these have been of a rather costly and in some cases 
palatial nature. Tftere has been little housing constructed for renting within the reach of persons of modest income.
Next, the prices of houses are still very high. The present prices place them beyond the reach of many people who are in need of housing.
Next, the down payment still remains very high. It is still too high for many people who need housing, and the extent of that down payment still depends, in large part at least, on the lending value determined by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
The maximum loan, of course, was increased when this act was brought into effect two years ago; in the case of any house constructed for owner occupancy, to $12,800.
Another feature which follows from the last one I have mentioned is that the provisions of the act in part I are being confined in their benefits more and more to persons with better than average incomes. The figures are rather significant. If you look at the average gross family income of home-owner borrowers you will see that in 1953 under the former act that average was $4,961. Those are the persons who have received the benefit of being able to borrow under the provisions of part I of the National Housing Act. In 1954, the year in which the new act was in effect for approximately eight months of the year the average gross family income of home-owner borrowers under part I had increased to $5,382. In 1955, for the first half of the year, that average gross family income had further increased to $5,447.
It is quite obvious that if those who are qualifying for loans under part I of the act to build owner-occupied houses are persons with an average family income at the middle of 1955 of $5,447, persons of modest income are deriving little or no benefit from the provisions of part I of this act. It seems to me that that is one of the serious problems which confront this house today in connection with the provisions of this act and its administration. If anyone here pretends that one of the purposes of this act is to provide assistance for persons of modest income in acquiring homes, then certainly that purpose is not being achieved. Under present conditions, under present provisions of the act and under present administration there just is not any chance whatever of that purpose being achieved. Let us look the facts in the face.
The next factor relates to inspections. When this legislation was under consideration two years ago some of us expressed grave concern that under the new insurance scheme there would be such centralization of inspections under Central Mortgage and Housing

Corporation that delays would be inevitable. Unhappily that has been the fact. The centralization of these inspections in Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has resulted in very long delays and increasing bureaucracy.
My next comment is with regard to the effective rate of interest charged or permitted under the various parts of the act, and in particular under part I dealing with the interest rate on mortgages on houses constructed for owner-occupancy. When the new act was brought into effect by proclamation on March 19, 1954, the effective rate was set by order in council 410 at 5J per cent per annum. On February 16, 1955, under order in council 213 that rate of interest was reduced by one-quarter of one per cent to 5i per cent. The rates under other parts of the act were likewise reduced one-quarter of one per cent. This was in keeping with the trend in interest rates throughout the country and in the face of an abundance of money available for mortgage lending.
On March 22, 1956 by order in council 466 the government has moved all of these interest rates up again by one-quarter of one per cent. The interest rates applicable to loans under part I of the act are now back at 5J per cent. I am led by this increase in the rate by government decision to ask: Is the government seeking to reduce the rate of house construction in Canada? One recalls the experience of 1950 when in the immediate post-Korea period the government sought to restrain house construction for a period of a year or two. If the government seeks today to restrain the rate of house construction then I think they ought to say so.
Certainly there was no such suggestion two years ago when the new act came into effect. On the contrary, the government indicated at that time that their hope and expectation as a result of the introduction of the insurance provision were that there would be an increase in the rate of house construction. There has been no statement from the government since to indicate any change in that policy or that outlook. Indeed the minister has taken some satisfaction out of the high rate of house construction in 1955 and its carryover into 1956. I recall that the Minister of Finance spoke to similar effect in his budget speech.
I am bound to point out that an increase in the interest rate normally has the effect and usually is intended to have the effect of restraining house construction. I think the minister owes it to the house to explain the evident contradiction between the policy of 67509-201
National Housing Act
his department in seeking to maintain a high volume of house construction, perhaps even to increase it, and the financial policy of the government in seeking to apply by fiscal measures restraint upon what they choose to call inflationary forces.
What is the government's thinking in this regard? The Minister of Finance does not come out and say frankly that the government is seeking by this increase in the interest rate to restrain house construction, but for what purpose is the increase in the interest rate put forward as it is as an antiinflationary measure? What purpose is it to serve in this context? It seems to me that barring a frank statement from the government we have here another example of befuddled thinking. There is evidence of contradiction in the policies of the two departments. Let us have from the government a clear statement of what its objective is and then we will be in a position to judge.
I should like to turn now to another matter. The act confers very wide powers upon Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and in this respect administration becomes increasingly more important as the act in a sense becomes more stabilized in its provisions. Administration can mean the difference between effectiveness in carrying out the provisions of the act for the purposes for which parliament intended them, on the one hand, and setting at nought, in part at least, the provisions of the act, on the other hand.
The act vests administration in Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation as the agent of the government and in this chamber the government must accept responsibility for the acts of administration, the omissions or failures of its agent. Therefore I think it is important at this point that we should give some thought to an examination of the administration.
In my observations upon that administration as I have sought to follow it I propose to test it by the experience in the city of Toronto. In the construction going on in that city and in the fringe about the metropolitan area there lies perhaps the widest opportunity in Canada today for testing the administration of the provisions of this act under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The conclusions which my review of that administration has led me to are that the corporation is becoming increasingly bureaucratic in its attitude and behaviour. There is increasing evidence of an ivory tower complex and in some respects that bureaucratic attitude is verging on the autocratic. The corporation is becoming more and more remote from the people and their problems.

speechtext:
I hope I shall have time to do that. I do not wish to take up a lot of time of the house, but if the house will permit me I should like to give examples, because I am just as concerned as is the minister to see the administration of the act made as effective for its intended purpose as is possible because, when the act was introduced and enacted, there was a wide measure of agreement in the house on its objectives. We may not all have shared quite the same expectations from different aspects of the changes, but it has always seemed to me that it was the earnest desire of the house that in enacting the provisions of this measure the utmost efficacy should be expected in their administration. I am saying what I am about to say now, not because I take any satisfaction in what I find in the attitude of the corporation, or those particular aspects of its attitude which I have mentioned, but in the hope that in saying something about them here it may perhaps have some corrective effect.
I was saying that it is evident that the corporation is becoming too remote from people and their thinking, that it is closing its ears to the thinking of the people and, to that extent, in its attitude is becoming unrealistic in many particulars. The result has been delays and the loss of valuable time with respect to projects that were undoubtedly urgent.
Now I should like to illustrate. I turn to the city of Toronto. I mention first of all the leading venture in the field of public low rental housing for all of Canada, for I conceive it so to be: the Regent Park North project. If the house will permit me, I should like to say I have had a personal interest in this matter since the year 1943. As a member of the city planning board in Toronto in that year I had with my colleagues on that board the privilege of fathering the first proposal for the redevelopment of the site on which the Regent Park North project was since constructed. I regard it as the outstanding success in public low-rent housing in Canada today. It cleared an area of 42 J acres, chiefly of blighted houses: the area bounded by Parliament, Gerrard, River and Dundas streets. The land assembly was carried out by the city of Toronto, and under the provisions of section 12 of the old act the federal government contributed half of the cost, that is to say, half the difference between the actual cost of the land assembly and the price at which it was turned over to the housing authority, which has managed it since. That was the only federal contribution to this project. This was not a project carried out under what later became section 35 of the 
Housing Act. It was a municipal project carried out with substantial assistance from the province of Ontario. As I say, the federal government's contribution was confined under section 12 to half of the cost of the land assembly.

speechtext: Could the hon. member say what year that was?

speechtext:
Of construction? Actually the first family moved in in April 1949, but the project was first put forward, I might repeat, in 1943. After the war there was a municipal plebiscite held on the question whether the city should proceed with it, and it was endorsed by the Toronto ratepayers. The management was placed under the Toronto housing authority. The Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has never had at any time, and has not today, any part whatever in the management and operation of this project.
Here is the record. When finally completed, by the end of this year there will be 1,289 housing units constructed, largely of the block apartment type. Only a few remain to be completed. Those units house approximately 5,000 people, including 2,000 children under the age of 16 years. I think the management has been conspicuously successful. The project has been fortunate in having as its manager Mr. Frank Dearlove, an official long in the service of the city of Toronto, with excellent experience and, I might say, great devotion to the success of this project.
I think it is an interesting answer to any who have inherent fears in regard to projects under ownership and management of this kind, that administrative costs to date have been less than five per cent of the revenue. Arrears of rent since the first family moved in, in April 1949, amount to just $68. That has indeed been a remarkable record. A recreational program is provided in the area under the city parks department. In my opinion, much of the undoubted and unchallenged success of this project has been due to citizen interest, and that is why I am so concerned that in projects undertaken, studied or managed by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation we should never lose any opportunity to maintain and encourage citizen interest. It is the healthiest factor that we can introduce in a situation of this kind, in my humble opinion.
In the first place, I have mentioned the plebiscite. It was brought before all of the Toronto voters. In the second place, the Toronto city council has maintained at all times an active interest in the project, its management and its success. The members

of the housing authority placed in charge have been devoted people, and 1 think a great deal of credit is due to them. However, in addition to these factors, there was a high measure of citizen interest maintained in particular by certain organizations. I mention in particular, because I well know of their interest and its beneficial results, the Women Electors Association. Here again, if you can get women citizens interested in a housing project and maintain their interest, I do not think you could have any healthier type of interest. One of the major contributions that the women electors association made to the success of this project was the service of the late Mrs. Bessie Luffman, a prominent member of the Women Electors Association, following her appointment as a member of the Toronto housing authority. Her death a few months ago terminated a life of high service to the cause of housing and other beneficial pursuits in the city of Toronto.
I bring this before the house now by way of illustration of some of the things that have happened since, with respect to other proposed projects where the course of development has not been nearly as happy as the record that I have just given.

I think the experience in all these cases has been that where a blighted area is redeveloped and reconstructed it is always possible to house more people in the area and house them infinitely better than you could before. That was the experience in the Regent Park North area. I shall say a word later about the matter of rents and the approach to them.
The Regent Park North project obviously forms a most valuable pilot project with respect to any similar undertakings, and I would commend it strongly to the government as such. But I do not find that the lessons derived from the success of that project have been applied too sympathetically by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
I come now to deal specifically with a proposed new project in an area lying immediately south of the area covered by the Regent Park North project. It is bounded by Dundas, River, Sydenham and Regent streets, and is known in Toronto as the Regent Park South project. It would involve the clearing of another blighted area for redevelopment. The city has been making excellent progress in acquiring the land for this purpose. As the partnership provisions of the new act now apply in dealing with blighted areas and their redevelopment, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is in effective control of the proposed redevelopment. But, unfortunately, the record of what has happened has been a record of delays. I wish to be fair about this. I do not say that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is entirely responsible for the delays, but I think a fair review of the record will show that the principal measure of responsibility does rest upon that corporation, and consequently the government must accept it.
Let me give some examples quickly in passing, because I do not wish to delay the committee, of what I think are evidences of rigidity in the attitude of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. It is inevitable, where any governmental body has power and administrative responsibility such as are cast upon Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation under legislation like this, that there develops a tendency, people being human, towards a bureaucratic approach. I am sure that the minister will be vigilant at all times and I urge him to be vigilant to correct any evidence of any growing attitude of that kind that he finds.
In the first place, whereas in Regent Park North construction proceeded on the basis of block apartments with very good results, what is proposed in connection with Regent

National Housing Act
Park South is tall apartments plus row housing. The reason given tor the construction of row housing is that they wish to have families with children on the ground level or close to it. But, sir, I point out that construction of a lot of row housing in that particular area in the old heart of the city is unrealistic. In time a lot of row housing is likely to turn into the old familiar terrace housing with small enclosed yards and houses with exposure only at the front and rear. I think there is a very grave danger that in years to come row housing is likely to give rise to blighted areas again, particularly when the management and upkeep of row housing will not be, to the same extent, at any rate, in the hands of those who have the responsibility for overseeing the project in other respects. The experienced officials of Regent Park North have recommended against row housing, but their advice has not been given effect to by those who are now carrying forward the proposed Regent Park South project.
In the second place, when Regent Park North was constructed enough boiler space was provided to heat the Regent Park South project today if it is proceeded with, and I am informed it was proposed to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation that it should be so used, but the proposal was rejected by that corporation. They insist upon separate heating facilities being provided for the Regent Park South project.
In the third place, I am informed that the administrative offices for the Regent Park North project are adequate for the provision of administrative services for the Regent Park South project, but that idea again has been rejected by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. They want the administrative offices for Regent Park South located in Regent Park South although the two areas are contiguous.
In the fourth place, there is the problem of management. I have no doubt that the very capable management that has made a success of the Regent Park North project could with a little encouragement assume the management of Regent Park South, but again I am informed that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation insists upon strictly separate management. The minister shakes his head. I can say to him that is my information. We must all agree, I think, that the success of these projects will depend upon the availability of well trained management personnel. That has been one of the major factors in the success of Regent Park North and I hope its importance will not be overlooked in connection with Regent Park South.
In the next place, I come to the matter of the income regulations with respect to the

occupants of these two respective housing projects. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has insisted upon a different basis of calculation in this respect. Let us look at the provisions that govern the determination of rents in the Regent Park North project. In the first place, income is determined on the basis of including the income of the head of the house and $10 per week for every other earner in the family. In the case of Regent Park South, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation insists on including the total income of all members of the family plus the family allowance. There you are creating a disparity at once and I think that some friction is necessarily bound to follow.
In the second place, in determining the maximum income permitted to occupants of Regent Park North $4,200 was the maximum determined except in the case of former residents of the area who were accorded priority. In the case of the proposed Regent Park South project the maximum is determined at $4,404.
Let us turn though to the minimum income provisions. In the case of Regent Park North no minimum income whatever was stipulated on the part of the housing authority. Indeed, an effort was made to use that project to meet need on the basis of need. In the case of the proposed Regent Park South project the regulations administered by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation require that every tenant must have a minimum income of $150 per month. In other words, need does not count. No person is going to be admitted to an apartment or a house in that project unless he has an income of $1,800 a year to begin with.
I understood, Mr. Chairman, that the reason that parliament was being asked to approve the provisions relating to federal-provincial partnership in connection with the redevelopment of blighted areas when we enacted the provisions of the new act in 1954 and the provision of the old section 35 of the National Housing Act some years earlier, and when we made substantial appropriations available for the purpose, was to meet a social need. We do not justify measures of this kind simply on the bare bones of economic considerations. We look at broader social considerations in approaching legislation of this kind.
Here we have a situation where an important project, being studied now as a project under federal-provincial partnership, is to have a term attached to it that will deny any occupancy in this project to any tenant who cannot satisfy Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation that he has an income of at

least $150 per month. Now, the effect of that is going to be to exclude everybody whose income is less than that. As I understand it, that is not carrying out the purpose for which parliament enacted this provision. If I do not correctly understand the purpose of parliament in adopting this provision, then I hope I will be corrected soon. A stipulation of this kind certainly does not carry out the intent of this legislation as I understand it to be.
Now, sir, all these differences introduced between the proposals for the Regent Park South project and the provisions attached to the successful Regent Park North project, have resulted in delays. I do not say Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is solely responsible for them, but I do say Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has not escaped a high measure of responsibility in connection with them. In particular, there has been no attempt to encourage the interest and participation of citizen groups. Indeed, some of the citizen groups that were most keenly interested in the Regent Park North project have developed a feeling now in response of the attitude of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is not interested in their participation; that it is taking a "hands off" attitude with respect to citizen interest. In any event the result of it all has been that there has been a discouragement of citizen interest. It is not enough that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation should put beautiful plans on paper. There are some things with respect to a project of this kind that are just as important, and in my opinion more important, and citizen interest on the part of intelligent civic groups is one of those more important considerations.
There is just one other matter I shall mention in conclusion. It is the experience of the Metropolitan Toronto Housing Company in connection with the proposed construction of a housing project for aged persons at Lawrence Heights in the suburbs of Toronto. This company is a limited dividend housing corporation organized by the Metropolitan Toronto Housing Authority, which set out to construct 128 suites for aged couples at a cost of $722,000. It was to be a low rent project in the township of Etobicoke. The result of long delays, for which again I believe the principal responsibility must rest, upon Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, has been that the whole project has now reached the point of frustration. This story was told in last Saturday's issue of the Globe and Mail by Lex Schrag. After inquiry I think I can say to the house that his review of the steps in this unhappy episode is fully justified by the facts.
National Housing Act
He said:
Looks as though red tape and metropolitan Toronto's fair wages practice could scupper Metropolitan Toronto Housing Company plans for senior citizens' low rent apartments in Etobicoke.
The company was formed two years ago. Metro had bought land in Etobicoke. The company bought sites from Metro for 128 apartments, and began dickering with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
It was expected CMHC would make a loan covering 90 per cent of the project's cost, recoverable over 50 years. First, though, CMHC wanted to know the cost. So an architect was engaged to draw plans and make an estimate.
Tenders were called, and the contract for the apartments was let to the lowest bidder. The contract was sent to CMHC at Ottawa. Got pigeonholed, and nothing happened for several months. After some pressure had been put on by Metro, officers, the plans were dug out of the pigeonhole-
A variety of CMHC supervisors and inspectors went over the project, and suggested minor restrictions and changes. Reams of correspondence were accumulated. Then it was decided that the contract was too low to conform to Metro's fair wages practice.
The original estimate had been based on the going price of similar structures in Toronto and so, apparently, had the accepted tender. Under the fair wages practice, Metro officials sit down with officers of the Toronto Builders' Exchange and union officials, and decide what labour costs and rates are to be.
The delay in getting work under way hadn't helped the project to conform to this practice, and the original estimate, apparently, wasn't based on all-union labour. So the housing company had to ask Metro for more money. And then CMHC said it would put up only 90 per cent of the original estimate.
Besides which, CMHC decided it wanted another 25 feet easement-or ground space-around the apartments. So back the company officers had to go to Metro.
Meantime, the contractor whose tender had been accepted was getting decidedly restive. He couldn't keep his men and equipment tied up for a job that didn't get going. It now looks as though the contractor will have to be released, and new tenders called.
So the story proceeds.
Now, sir, I have brought these matters to the attention of the house because of the concern that I am sure all hon. members share that measures enacted by parliament shall, in their administration, be made effective for the purpose for which parliament enacted them. Here, it seems to me, is a case where Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has fallen into some errors which are perhaps natural temptations attending any governmental body under such circumstances. But we can see the results of too much rigidity; too much bureaucracy; too much of the ivory tower complex; too much of the feeling that the experts in the ivory tower know more than the citizens who are on the spot and face the situation firsthand.
In raising these matters here today, I do not do so with any degree of satisfaction. I do so

National Housing Act
rather in the hope that, with the assistance of the minister, measures will be taken to correct this attitude and to see that no delays are permitted to arise that are attributable to rigidity and a bureaucratic approach. Rather let us hope that a frank review of the administration as we see it in a concrete situation

and this is the first opportunity we have had in two years for that purpose, -and what is said in the house may act in some degree as a spur upon the responsible officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and that they may be encouraged to put behind their duties in administering the provisions of this act the fullest determination to make these provisions effective for the purposes for which parliament enacted them.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTRIBUTIONS TO MUNICIPALITIES, HOME LOANS, HOUSING RESEARCH, ETC.
speechtext:
When the National Housing Act was before parliament in the session of 1953-54, Mr. Chairman, the C.C.F. members made certain objections to certain aspects of the legislation, pointing out their inadequacy and the failure of the act to meet the housing needs of the average Canadian citizen. Hon. members will recall, and I think our members were refreshed the other evening when the minister once again had all members of the house rise and be counted on a particular bill, that at the time the National Housing Act was passed, he made rather caustic comments about the critics of the legislation. The time which has elapsed since the passage of the present National Housing Act has vindicated the criticism which we made at that time. Indeed, we have found that the case if anything was a little understated.
In speaking in the budget debate the other day I placed on record a table showing the participation by various income groups under the National Housing Act, and without labouring that particular point I wish to point out that since 1948 the percentage of those in the relatively high income groups under the National Housing Act has gone up while, on the other hand, the percentage of those in the relatively lower income groups has gone down, so that the criticism which we made to the effect that few, if any, Canadians earning less than $3,800 a year would benefit under part I of the National Housing Act, has certainly been substantiated in the intervening period of time. Indeed, we find that of Canadians earning less than $3,500 a year there are somewhere in the neighbourhood of 4 per cent who have obtained any benefit whatever from part I of the National Housing Act.

It seems to me that when we are discussing the resolution now before us we have to consider the housing need and the likelihood of the legislation proposed by the government making any worth-while attack on the problem. We have to provide for home ownership wherever possible, and, of course, that is not being done as far as low income groups are concerned under the present part I of the National Housing Act. It seems to me that the greater percentage of Canadians ought to be in a position where they can purchase their own houses. It is quite clear that under the present National Housing Act that is not possible for a great percentage of Canadian citizens. If those Canadians who are earning possibly now under $4,000 a year are unable to benefit from part I of the National Housing Act, then it is quite obvious that some other measures are going to have to be taken if we are to see that our Canadian people are adequately housed.
We have suggested on numerous occasions that what we need in Canada, apart from a program to provide for greater home ownership, is legislation to provide for low-rental housing for the vast number of Canadians who by the nature of their jobs are not in a position to establish themselves permanently in one locality, or are not in a position to purchase a house at the present time. I know that the resolution before the house states that this measure is designed for the further improvement of housing and living conditions. Inasmuch as the resolution seeks to explore and to do something about this broad question of housing, it is the type of legislation we are anxious to see proceeded with at the present time. But we are going to have to put the same test to this proposed legislation as we did when the amendments to the National Housing Act were brought down in 1954. We are going to have to examine the housing picture in Canada and see how closely the legislation comes to meeting the needs of the Canadian people at the present time.
One thing I think we should settle at the outset is that housing is not merely an economic problem; more and more Canadians are beginning to realize that housing is a major social problem. Indeed, in the very excellent brief presented by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospect they state in chapter 2:
Because of its fundamental place in a modern industrial economy and because of its deep social implications, housing is a matter in which governments at all levels are inevitably and intimately involved. The provision of housing has some of

the aspects of a public service, inviting governmental participation and community action for reasons of economic policy and in pursuit of welfare objectives.
Therefore, we cannot consider the housing program from purely economic aspects. We have to consider the necessity of doing something about our shocking housing situation in this country from the aspect of social welfare and the effect it is going to have on the health and happiness of the Canadian people. Humphrey Carver, in his book, "Houses for Canadians", brings out the point I think quite clearly. He says:
The severity of the housing shortage must be measured in terms of human distress. Children and adults crowded into small quarters cannot escape from the frictions and frustrations occasioned by too close and too constant proximity. The humiliation, squalor and ugliness of obsolete and temporary housing leave their permanent mark upon the occupants.
All sorts of evidence has been advanced as to the social implications of housing and the folly of continuing to ignore this basic problem. Indeed, public health officers from one end of Canada to the other have from time to time emphasized the importance of housing on public health. The medical health officer in the city of Regina, in his annual reports to council, has placed great stress on housing conditions and on more than one occasion has described housing as the biggest health problem in the world today. Indeed, one cannot separate inadequate housing from the general problems of social welfare and public health; hence, any program designed to alleviate our housing problem is also one that is going to meet in large measure social welfare and health needs in Canada.
Of course, this is not something new. As far back as 1943 the Curtis report emphasized time and time again the social implications of poor housing and pointed out the incidence of tuberculosis in good housing areas was 25 per 10,000 population, while it was 64 per 10,000 in poor housing areas. The same situation applies in so far as infant mortality rates are concerned. They were 58-3 per thousand live births in good housing areas and 121-8 per thousand live births in poor housing areas, which is a shocking waste of human life, much of which could be prevented if decent housing conditions prevailed.
John Boyd Orr, in his excellent pamphlet entitled, "Housing and Health", quotes a United States investigator who stated that after a very close examination of both British and United States health statistics, the death rate from nervous and nutritional diseases showed a fivefold difference in areas
National Housing Act
where people were adequately housed as compared with slum areas.
In the field of juvenile delinquency the social problems were so immense that they could only be met by doing something about our housing situation in Canada. I believe that we as a parliament should be setting forth cur ultimate objective for a housing program. You know, there are too many people in the country who look upon the housing problem in terms of meeting an economic demand in the typical free enterprise fashion. They say, "Well, here is a particular need, and we are out to meet the need", as determinated by the ability of the people to pay a particular price at a given time for a certain commodity. The argument is that there are so many people in Canada who at present-day market prices are able to buy homes and therefore if you meet that demand the problem has been solved. I suggest that we have to look at the problem from an entirely different point of view, that the ultimate goal of a proper housing policy for Canada should be the provision of modern, structurally separate dwelling units of adequate size and decent quality for every family household and individual requiring them.
As I pointed out, the major flaw in the thinking of many government leaders today is that they continue to think of housing purely in terms of economics, failing to take into consideration the wider social aspects of this great problem.
We in the C.C.F. certainly believe that housing should be based on actual needs and that a supply of housing ought to be dependent on the requirements of those who at present are in need of adequate housing.
During my talk on the budget I referred to the fires which had occurred in the Ottawa area and throughout the country generally during the past few months and suggested that a great deal of this shocking loss of life could have been averted if something had been done to provide more adequate housing. Indeed, many of the most serious fires have occurred in substandard dwellings where there is faulty wiring and there are faulty heating units. The only way in which we are going to provide for a greater measure of safety against the recurring loss of life from fires is to provide homes built according to certain minimum requirements. These requirements would include adequate and proper heating units and wiring, and so forth. Until we do that we are going to be continually faced with this problem of loss of life as a result of fires.

National Housing Act
Now, Mr. Chairman, in assessing the housing problem in Canada at this time I was quite interested in the joint submission placed before the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects by the trades and labour congress of Canada and the Canadian congress of labour. In the section dealing with housing in their excellent brief, they point out that there are three aspects to the housing problem in Canada.
First, of course, is the question: What is the housing need and how many dwelling units are required in Canada at the present time? Second, what is the physical capacity of Canada's building industry? Third, what is the ability of Canadians to purchase housing?
As far as the first aspect is concerned, I think one must recognize that there are two factors to consider. The first of these is the annual need for houses to take care of net growth of new families in any one year. Second, we must consider the need to replace dwellings which have been removed during the year through fire or demolition.
The brief presented by the two labour congresses suggests that there are about
85,000	new units required each year in order to meet this first demand; that is, the annual economic demand for new houses. In addition to that there is a tremendous backlog of housing which will have to be met if we wish to make any frontal attack on our housing problem.
There may be some dispute as to the actual size of this backlog, but the joint labour brief suggests that there is a need for approximately 500,000 new dwellings plus the need for some 123,000 dwellings to replace rural dwellings in substandard condition. It might be said that the maximum figure suggested is somewhere in the neighbourhood of 623,000.
We know that the greatest portion of this need will be to take care of the vast number of Canadians who are doubled up; that is, who are living not as single family units but with in-laws or friends through economic necessity. It is computed that it would require some 370,000 new dwellings in order to provide single unit dwellings for Canadian families in the urban areas of this country. In addition to the 370,000 dwellings required to meet that particular need there would be in the neighbourhood of 140,000 units necessary to replace urban substandard or slum housing.
If you add those figures you will find that they total over half a million, representing the number of dwellings which are needed in Canada. If you add to that the number of

substandard rural dwellings which will have to be replaced, you would have to add another 123,000, thus making a grand total of 623,000 dwellings.
As far as the doubling up is concerned, I note that a few years ago Mr. Mansur suggested a certain amount of this doubling up was voluntary. In the brief submitted to the royal commission by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, however, they do admit quite candidly that the doubling up is not through choice but is rather through economic necessity. Indeed, the congresses' brief places on record certain statistics which prove quite conclusively that those families with low incomes are the ones forced to live in overcrowded conditions and to share accommodation with other families.
The brief points out that where the head of a family is earning over $6,000 a year the percentage of families not maintaining separate households was only 1-43 per cent; for those with an income of $4,000 to $6,000, it was 3 [DOT] 1 per cent; for those earning between $3,000 and $4,000, it was 6-17 per cent; for those earning $2,000 to $3,000, it was 10-64 per cent; for those in the $1,000 to $2,000 bracket it was 14-7 per cent and for those receiving less than $1,000 it was 19-46. In other words the lower the income, the greater is the economic pressure on families to double up and share accommodation. I think anyone can readily see from the standpoint of public health alone that this situation is not one which should commend itself to the government.
In relation to the figure of 623,000 which I suggested represents the number of dwellings necessary each year to take care of our natural growth, perhaps one should make certain allowances. There might be a few families who prefer to live doubled up. Also, there may be some dwellings which are slated for replacement but which with extensive alterations and repairs might be made habitable again. But even making allowances for these factors I think one could agree with the joint labour brief that 400,000 dwellings is the barest minimum of the housing backlog facing the country at the present time. At the present rate of home construction, bearing in mind the number of starts and completions last year, it would take 10 years to counteract that backlog. I suggest that the legislation which the government is bringing forward must do something to accelerate the elimination of this tremendous backlog.
In dealing with the question of Canada's physical capacity to meet our housing problem I thought that two years ago the minister suggested that we have a capacity for around
135,000	dwellings per year.

I think the figure would seem to be quite accurate. I understand that last year there were 138,000 starts and some 128,000 completions, which indicates that last year we did meet the yearly requirement so far as housing is concerned and nibbled away to some small extent on the backlog to which I have been referring. However, a great deal will have to be done if we are going to bring about some amelioration of the conditions existing in the country at the present time.
Of course the major factor is the ability of people to pay for housing. I have dealt with part I of the National Housing Act and have pointed out that under its terms anyone earning under $4,000 a year could not hope to benefit under the provisions of the act. I think the latest figures reveal that the cheapest N.H.A. house is something in the neighbourhood of $11,700. If that figure were amortized over a period of 25 years at the present rate of interest it would require an individual having an income of at least $4,000 in order to enter into a contract to purchase a home under that particular section.
I repeat my question: What is the government proposing to do to extend the provisions of this act to those who earn lower incomes? Does the government feel that home ownership is primarily the prerogative of those who earn $4,000 a year or more, or does it feel that some measure should be taken to provide home ownership for those earning incomes much lower than the present minimum figure required under the N.H.A.?
It seems to me that that is the crux of the problem. We have to provide home ownership possibilities for a much greater number of Canadian citizens than are provided for at the present time. For those whom we cannot serve from the standpoint of home building or home purchasing some provision will have to be made in the way of low rental housing. If that entails an element of subsidy, then we must face up to that question. Apparently we have no hesitation in subsidizing business generally. Our tariff structure is perhaps the biggest form of subsidy in existence. This house has been called upon to subsidize the gold mining industry, the argument being that a whole segment of the population is vitally concerned. Surely housing is important enough that the government should consider the absolute necessity of providing a greater measure of assistance for those in the low income brackets.
I realize that sections 16 and 36 of the National Housing Act contain certain possibilities, but I would remind the minister that
National Housing Act
while the rentals possible in connection with low rental housing projects may seem low to a great many Canadians-it would seem a low rental to many of us-I am sure that there are many Canadians to whom $58 or $60 a month would not be a low rent. Certainly it is low in comparison with $125 or $150 a month. Low rentals, such as would be possible under section 16, are simply relative. To a vast number of Canadians such rentals would represent a high rent.
The minister will recall that when the N.H.A. was under discussion before I referred to a project in the city of Ottawa and I quoted from an editorial which had appeared in the Ottawa Citizen which pointed out that even if that project were completed it would not meet the needs of a great many Ottawa citizens whose salaries are quite low, that they would not be able to qualify for accommodation in that particular project. A few minutes ago the hon. member for Eglinton pointed out that the limits set on occupancy in particular low rental housing projects denied access to a great many low income earning Canadians.
It seems to me that we have to accelerate our program and shift the emphasis from assistance for those with relatively high incomes-I use the word "relatively" because there is a difference of opinion as to what constitutes high income-and in this connection I agree wholeheartedly with the joint submission by the labour congresses to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects, and I quote from page 115 as follows:
But we are most strongly in favour of more public, subsidized low-rental housing under section 36. More of this is urgently needed. This, and cooperative housing, are the only methods which will provide decent housing for the people who need it most. On the whole, hitherto, our national housing policy has concentrated on helping people of moderate, or more than moderate, income. It is time for a shift in emphasis.
We now have before us a resolution purporting to bring about an improvement in housing and living conditions in Canada. There are six sections to this resolution but even with the minister's statement we do not know what is involved. We shall watch carefully to see whether the government is taking cognizance of the need for assistance to Canadians in the low income brackets. It is all very well to boast, as the minister did earlier in the session, about the number of starts made last year and the fact that we are now finally catching up to current needs, but so far the government has done little or nothing to provide for the housing needs of Canadians with low incomes. We shall watch this proposed legislation most carefully. I want to ask the government whether it has learned

National Housing Act
from its experience under the previous legislation and whether it now realizes the necessity of shifting the emphasis toward the provision of housing for those people in Canada who need it most.

Mr. Chairman, we in this group welcome the opportunity of again being able to discuss Canada's housing legislation. In 1953 when the housing act was first reintroduced for a complete revision we expressed our opinion that the act did not meet the needs of the people. From what I have heard of the discussion up to now I am not too satisfied that this present resolution is going to do a great deal more in that respect.
I was interested in what the hon. member for Regina City had to say because I agree with what he says about low rental housing. However, I wonder whether the figure of
623.000	as the number of dwellings being required is a true statement of fact.
