subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTRIBUTIONS TO MUNICIPALITIES, HOME LOANS, HOUSING RESEARCH, ETC.
speechtext:
I am not questioning the fact that 623,000 dwellings are required in Canada. I am just questioning whether they took into consideration the fact that thousands of people today do not want houses under the National Housing Act. They want to own their own homes, and they want to own them completely, without owing anybody. I do know that the Canadians of former years certainly wanted to build homes and I am satisfied that they did not want to borrow money to do so. I would say that the figure of 623,000 would be quite accurate if they could get homes at the prices at which they want them and are willing to pay for them, and with the down payment which they are prepared to make on them.
I am not disputing the fact that we could use 623,000 new homes. We could probably use more than a million new homes if every person in this country who owns a home were asked if he would like to replace it with a better one. But there are thousands of people living in homes today-some of the
623.000	referred to by the hon. member for Regina City-who, if you asked them specifically whether they wished to change their homes for new ones and go into debt for $6,000 or $7,000, would say offhand that they were not interested. They would say, "We want to own our home. We own this one and we are not interested in going into debt any further at this time."
However, that does not exonerate this government from the responsibility it has with

respect to the low-rental homes in this country. In 1953 I spoke to the resolution, and at that time I indicated that I felt there was a large group of home owners in this country who needed legislation that would cover financial assistance for home improvements that was not being afforded under the terms of that act and that would be desirable in so far as they were concerned. I think I repeated that argument later when the act was again brought before us for revision. Now I feel satisfied that in this present resolution and the explanation I heard I find very little that would indicate that this is going to be taken care of.
Speaking specifically to the resolution, I see in paragraph (a) that we have the following: ... to provide for payments of contributions to municipalities in order to assist in the clearance, replanning, rehabilitation and modernization of blighted areas, . . .
That is most desirable, so much so, in fact, that I would endorse it 100 per cent; but I am not satisfied that under our present scheme of things it is going to be taken advantage of very freely, by reason of the fact that the municipalities that should take advantage of the act are those which are growing most rapidly. They are in the unfortunate position of not having sufficient funds to do that very thing. They are the municipalities that are actually more in need of financial assistance, rather than giving it to anyone else.
The reason for that is quite obvious. Their populations are growing very rapidly, and therefore there is a greater demand for public utilities and public services in those particular areas. They require new sewage works, more sidewalks, roads and policing and the other services that we find in these communities. The people in those areas, because they are progressing so rapidly, are those who are spending more in income tax, and the corporations are spending more in corporation tax. Of course when the inhabitants die they usually have more money; therefore more death duties as well are collected. Those very communities are sacrificing in two ways. They represent the wealthier sections of the country. That is where you have tfie greatest need for housing. Financially they are turning more and more money into the coffers of the federal government and are receiving less and less in return.
It seems to me that these areas certainly want to help all the other areas. There is no denying that. But they require a greater degree of assistance when it comes to making it possible to alleviate the housing conditions within their own areas, largely by reason of the fact that I indicated earlier, that they are the quickest growing and represent the wealthier districts within the country but,

because of our equalization of taxation laws, they are also in the most difficult position.
These municipalities do not know where to get the money. When I listen time and time again to the pleas for more housing and more money from this government, or any other government for that matter, I wonder exactly what the source of this revenue is going to be, unless we change our economic methods within this country. I would say that some recognition must be made of that.
I was thinking particularly along the line indicated by the hon. member for Regina City with respect to getting this financial assistance. We have members in this house who damn this government and anybody who considers that United States capital should come into the country. If we as taxpayers are going to build pipe lines with Canadian capital, build up our industries with Canadian capital, and try to build our houses as well, with a program such as was outlined by the hon. member for Regina City-and in this connection they will probably speak in this debate along the lines that we need 623,000 dwellings in this country-I am satisfied we are going to have to change our economics. It is just not possible to carry on in the present fashion of saying no to investment capital and anyone else who is trying to help us in one way or another.
I was thinking particularly-and I noticed this with some interest and some anguish, I might say when I read it-of an item in the Vancouver Province of Saturday, April 21, on page 23. I just want to refer to one paragraph, because it would have such a detrimental effect upon housing if that is what the hon. member thinks. This is an article datelined Washington, D.C. It states:
What's the fuss about U.S. "imperialism"?
. . . They are considering, as in the commerce department, whether the U.S. government shouldn't publicly advise American businessmen of the extent of that feeling in Canada against U.S. control of industry, and advise some judicious methods for dealing with the problem.
If we are going to refuse that, then where are we going to get money to help our housing schemes along? I say that is the most important factor and must be kept in mind all the time. These things are interrelated and they must be remembered as such.
I turn to paragraph (b) of the resolution. It says:
-to increase the aggregate amount of home improvement loans that may be guaranteed, from one hundred and twenty-five million dollars to two hundred million dollars;
Of course that would naturally follow, in view of the fact that we have this modification in the earlier part of the resolution, if
National Housing Act
it is taken advantage of and we have further investment in housing in the area. I am wondering whether the minister would, in the course of his answers, indicate to the house what effect the insurance clause has in the act itself and whether or not we have lost much-we would not have lost, of course, but whether there was much demand on the insurance fund-

speechtext:
-and the exact sum that was involved, in view of the effectiveness of that legislation for the past year or two and the fact that we have an insurance clause which carries a high interest and which provides that the premiums will be paid or that the rents will be paid. Then I should like to know, since we have such a buoyant economy, whether the fund had any drawings on it whatsoever.
The fourth part of the resolution has to do with housing research and community planning. That too is very important. The hon. member for Regina City mentioned that many homes were destroyed by fire during the past year. That is a most unfortunate condition and one that in my opinion is not absolutely necessary. However, no matter what our housing regulations may be, there is an onus of responsibility upon the householder himself. I am satisfied that the minister or his officials cannot go about the country policing homes in order to see that householders do not overload their electrical circuits and outlets with too many appliances.
So far as the construction of new homes is concerned, we as legislators have a responsibility to see to it that inspections are made to ascertain whether or not the regulations are being complied with, so as to be absolutely certain that new homes are as fireproof as possible. We should see to it that there is as much non-inflammable construction as possible, foolproof electrical conduits, simplified heating and everything else that will prevent a recurrence of the fires that took place in the Ottawa region and in Ontario last year which caused millions of dollars of damage. That is a most important fundamental in the building of new homes.
So far as old houses are concerned, advantage should be taken by people of the new act, and the only way that can be done is to make its provisions known as widely as possible to those citizens who own old homes. I am sure that many of these people, if funds are made available to them at a nominal rate of interest and they are given a longer period of time in which to repay, would take advantage of the provisions of the legislation to change the wiring of their

National Housing Act
homes so as to make it possible for it to carry the load it is expected to carry. We probably would not have a repetition of the disastrous fires we have had during the past year. Our responsibility does not end with the amending of the legislation. We have a greater responsibility to let people know that the act is being changed and that it will be possible for them to take advantage of its provisions to alter their homes in such a way as to make them safer.
I am satisfied, Mr. Chairman, that the minister has received certain correspondence from such organizations as the Vancouver housing association drawing his attention to the plight of many citizens in the poorer groups who are unable to house themselves properly. I refer to old age pensioners, our senior citizens, those who come specifically within the low income bracket. Those individuals and others with incomes of $4,000 a year or less are the ones who require a greater degree of help. I have, for instance, an editorial from the Vancouver Province of December 14, 1955, headed, "Needed-An Under $10,000 House". In my estimation that is one of the greatest needs in housing development today. We need such homes for the proper housing of people in the low income group, houses that will be built according to proper specifications. Incidentally, I am quite satisfied that if the research bureau were to investigate the matter further they would find that it was practical and possible to build a house to meet the specifications set out under the National Housing Act and which would at the same time cost less than $10,000. The editorial reads in part as follows:
Amendments to the National Housing Act next year-
That is this year.
-will take the emphasis off suburban building and encourage the reconstruction of older areas inside the cities. This is good. It is good for the suburban municipalities, which have been struggling to keep up with the demands for roads, water mains, schools, policing and all the other services for subdivisions that have been sprouting like mushrooms.
Dealing with that portion of the editorial, the very fact that the suggestion has been made that we should now rehabilitate certain sections of our cities where for various reasons houses have fallen into a state of disrepair merely indicates the necessity of taking advantage of the existing facilities. In this case the water mains are already there, the roads are there, the sidewalks are there and the sewage disposal units are there. Yet these sections of our cities are not being used to the best advantage. It becomes necessary that these areas should be used to better

advantage. Every available plot of ground must be used to advantage in these areas that are growing so rapidly. Possibly certain areas should be used, and rightfully so, for recreational purposes.
However, as I indicated earlier there has been a tremendous growth in the suburban areas in those parts of the nation where there the degree of growth has been greater possibly because of prosperity, and those areas are in great need of assistance. Possibly we can cut down the amount of that assistance by rebuilding certain of the older areas where facilities are already available. The editorial goes on to say:
By and large, N.H.A. has operated until now at the two ends of the housing scale. It has built homes for the ranch style and patio set with incomes of $6,000 and upwards, and it has done a certain amount to encourage community housing for those with low earnings or small pensions.
The words used there are "a certain amount to encourage community housing." That part of the editorial again causes me to pause, because I feel that therein lies the greatest need that we face in Canada today. I should like to refer to a recent issue of the Vancouver Province, that of Saturday, April 21. On page 18 there are some photographs of various homes in the Vancouver area showing what national housing has done. Underneath there is an article by Jack McCaugherty entitled, "Tiny Pensions Doom
42,000	to Live in Unfit B. C. Hovels." That, Mr. Chairman, is an indictment of the people of this country. Why should this newspaper, which has a circulation of over 300,000, be in the position of being able to tell the people of this country that some 42,000 people are doomed to live in unfit British Columbia homes? I do not intend to read the whole article, but the first portion of it is as follows:
Thousands of Vancouver's older citizens are tucking themselves away in the dark corners of the city, forced into run-down housing that isn't fit to live in. They have no choice. Their pensions won't buy anything better. Like the old lady who lived in a backyard garage without water and plumbing. The snow blew in through wallboards during winter. She had to share the bathroom in the landlord's house. If the landlord went away for the week end, the house was locked up, and with it the toilet facilities.
Or like the basement "suite" that rented for $35 a month with windows so small the lights had to be left on all day. And when it rained, the entrance was flooded, and pensioner tenants had to wade in.
Or the old woman who lived in a former stable. In cold weather the landlord shut off the water, fearing the pipes might freeze and burst. But rent was still $20 a month.
These are cases recently checked in Vancouver by housing groups.
They are examples of the plight of thousands of almost-forgotten senior citizens who with limited

income are forced to take dark, damp, unserviced quarters that give little comfort for their declining years.
A few non-profit societies have given this area some comfortable low-rent units for aged citizens. But the projects don't begin to meet the need.
Now, Mr. Chairman, that article is selfexplanatory, so I shall not comment upon it any further. I would only suggest to the minister that he take into consideration not just the economics of the situation, as was suggested by the hon. member for Regina, not just the fact that we need 623,000 homes in this country, but the fact that we do require homes as quickly as possible for a certain group of citizens who are, practically speaking, being starved to death. I daresay many of these people have found an undesirable way out. These people need attention, and the best attention we can give them today is to make a home available to them that will be a credit to our nation.
One paragraph in the brief which the minister is supposed to have received from the Vancouver housing association in October, 1955, reads as follows:
With the removal of rent controls in British Columbia, the following rent increases demanded of pensioners were reported:	From $25 to $42.50
(widow), from $21 to $45 (couple), from $25 to $42.50 (widower), from $17 to $30 (widow).
Some of these people in British Columbia are more fortunate in that they are eligible to get assistance under the means test. They may get as high as $60 per month. If the rents paid by these people compare with the rents paid by the people in other parts of Canada, then they do have too little left upon which to live. The brief goes on to say:
Any steps taken to increase the supply of low rental housing for this group will at the same time increase the real value of the pension and reduce the pressure of demand for a higher pension.
I am satisfied, Mr. Chairman, that if the minister were to discuss this subject with the Minister of National Health and Welfare he would find that gentleman in agreement with the view that if the housing authority could possibly make homes available to these elderly people at low rentals, then the demands for a higher pension would be somewhat offset by the amount which these people had left to buy their food and clothing.
Then there is another group which is mentioned in this brief and to which I should like to draw the minister's attention, as he may wish to make some comment about
National Housing Act
them. I refer to the families in receipt of social assistance. One paragraph in this brief says:
Average rents paid by families in receipt of social allowance in the city of Vancouver are considerably in excess of the minimum rental payable by working families admitted to public housing projects.
Note the significance of that, sir. The rental paid by these people is considerably in excess of the minimum rental payable by working families, yet these people are on social assistance and the taxpayers are helping to pay that rent. The brief says:
Yet for these rents they can often only obtain accommodation which jeopardizes their physical and mental wellbeing. A recent sample study of families of three persons or more in receipt of social allowance in the city of Vancouver showed that nearly half were living in accommodation which was seriously substandard or overcrowded.
Therein, Mr. Chairman, lies the problem we have today in respect of housing. I would submit that we do have to use our research branch to plan our communities with only one thought in mind at this time, and that is to see that these people in the lower income groups have housing made available to them at low rentals. I must conclude by saying that what Canada needs is a serviceable $6,000 to $8,000 home.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTRIBUTIONS TO MUNICIPALITIES, HOME LOANS, HOUSING RESEARCH, ETC.
speechtext:
I welcome this opportunity to say a few words to this committee, and I endorse the general remarks which were made by the hon. member for Eglinton. It is my intention to call particular notice to the housing conditions in suburban areas rather than to discuss the details of construction in the cities. I notice that the principle behind this resolution is to further improve the housing and living conditions in this country. Obviously, we are all in favour of any measure which will improve those conditions. My principal concern is whether the present resolution foretells a bill which will go far enough to meet the situation as it exists now.
During the Easter recess when I visited my constituency, large numbers of people made representations to me expressing concern over the housing situation. This number included not only the reeves of municipalities but also representatives of service clubs, bankers, real estate agents and those who were home seekers.
Immediately following the cessation of hostilities at the end of world war II there was a large number of homes constructed on Vancouver island. After a year or two the rate of building and the granting of permits declined. According to the figures I have available the lowest ebb was reached in 1951. Since that date the curve has been rising

National Housing Act steadily, with the result that today the level is back to the rush year of 1946 and demand is as high as ever.
While the demand is high it must also be noted that the price of the home has also increased. The cost of home construction on Vancouver island today is at least one-third greater than it was in 1946. This results from increased cost of labour and materials, the rising value of land, the cost of surveying and the cost of providing the various services. The result is that loans under the National Housing Act are no longer available to the individual of moderate means.
When I say the individual of moderate means, I am referring to employees at the shipping yards, for instance, the dockyards of Victoria and even municipal employees. I have an instance of a police constable who was in steady employment at $300 a month, but he failed to qualify for a loan which he required-it was quite a moderately priced house-because he was not able to come within the 23 per cent ratio. In fact the increased costs due, as I said before, to the cost of labour and materials, are putting a great many would-be house owners out of line and out of reach of a national housing loan. Every time there is an increase in the mortgage payments a few more people are put out of reach of those loans. It is all very well to say that in certain cases you will allow a little more than the 23 per cent, but that does not really compensate for those astonishing costs of construction.
One thing which has sent the cost of construction sky high is the requirement of certain specifications as laid down in the regulations. These specifications seem to have been drawn up on a national basis and are not sufficiently flexible for the particular agents of Central Mortgage and Housing to adjust to the various locations across the country. The same kind of construction is not necessary on Vancouver island as is required in the colder parts of Canada. When you find that in a small house of 850 square feet with a basement you are asked to put insulation in the basement walls it adds to the cost, and it is quite unnecessary in the milder climate of Vancouver island. Therefore I feel that something should be done to adjust those specifications in order to make them more applicable to the different parts of the country.
In my constituency at the present time there is a great demand for additional houses. Many of the people want small houses rather than a larger type of house which seems to be required by Central Mortgage and Housing. The price of a small house, if it meets all the specifications which are demanded by Central


Mortgage and Housing, soon gets out of reach of people who are anxious to live in suburban districts. We find that some of the larger estates which had acreages of from three, five to seven acres surrounding them are now being divided up. The children are grown up and have gone to live elsewhere, and the house has become too much for the elderly couple to maintain. They would like to divide up the estate, or perhaps it is a farm in the fringe area between the rural part of the island and the urban home districts.
When these estates or farms are subdivided, the purchasers make inquiries as to whether it is possible for them to obtain a national housing loan on the property. All too frequently they are told it is not possible because the area is not being serviced. No sewers are laid in that area. The district may be several miles away from the central part of Victoria. The lots may be of considerable extent, an acre, or something of that nature, but still they are not approved areas because there is no prospect of sewerage being established in the area, and septic tanks will not be approved.
Of course if someone wants to build a house without getting a National Housing Act loan there is no objection to their building and using a septic tank; but in those small subdivisions which are being offered there is the restriction that they cannot have a National Housing Act loan until sewerage has been put in. The municipalities simply have not the funds to develop those fringe areas with the services required.
Therefore it seems to me that something is required more than is indicated in this resolution, some legislation which will enable and encourage the building of small houses in the suburban areas, something which will give the opportunity either to the company that is going to develop the subdivision or the municipality to put in the requisite services. Frequently in my district water has been laid on. There is plenty of water available, but there is not the opportunity to put in the sewerage system that is required because of the heavy rock formation.
Then there seems to be a tendency on the part of Central Mortgage and Housing actually to discourage the building of houses. People are in need of accommodation. It is of little use to say, "You may build a house in the already built-up area" when the individual requires a house in the suburban area. The tendency seems to be to insist upon every vacant lot being built upon in the urban areas before any assistance will be given to the construction of houses in the suburban areas.

An impression is created in the district of greater Victoria that houses in the suburban areas are being discouraged because Central Mortgage and Housing have taken over a large tract of land in the city of Victoria which was at one time reserved for an airport. The particular land is not attractive from the point of view of ideal residences. It is rather low-lying and flat. While it would be very suitable for business construction, it is not the type of location that the majority of people who are anxious to build houses on some part of Vancouver island desire. If these suburban or fringe areas are being discriminated against in order that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation may dispose of their lots in the area which is known as Lansdowne park airport, I feel that is not right. There should be an easing of the strict restrictions which are now placed on the construction of small subdivisions which have been developed in the Gordon Head area, around Royal Oak and along the Wilkinson road.
It is particularly the problem of home construction in the suburban areas which I wish to draw to the attention of the minister this afternoon.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTRIBUTIONS TO MUNICIPALITIES, HOME LOANS, HOUSING RESEARCH, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was one of those who two years ago took a rather dim view of the National Housing Act to the extent of voting against it, because I felt at that time that the act as then presented to the house was not going to deal with the real housing problems of the Canadian people.
I would have been pleased, Mr. Chairman, if by now, after that act has been in operation for two years, I could have been proved wrong and that the housing needs of the Canadian people had actually been met. Unfortunately, of course, that is not the case.
I was interested in reading the tenth annual report of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to find on the first page this paragraph:
The Canadian people have shown an unmistakable preference for the single detached house as a place in which to raise a family and to spend leisure time. The possession of a house and a piece of land has been an aspiration and a motive in life. Fortunately the earning power and the productive capacity of the nation have made it possible for a new generation of Canadians to realize this desire. About 70 per cent of new housing has been in the form of home ownership.
That is rather interesting, Mr. Chairman, when we consider that the houses of the type which are built under the National Housing Act are, as has been commented upon several times this afternoon, confined to those people with incomes of $3,600 or more a year. I find on looking at the figures
National Housing Act
brought out by the bureau of statistics that the vast majority of the Canadian people do not fall into that category at all. I looked at the list of the various categories of incomes, and deciding to bend over backward to be perfectly fair about this I eliminated those getting incomes of less than $1,000 a year for the purpose of this discussion, because I imagine that the bulk of these are young people in their first jobs probably living at home. They are not likely to be the ones who are building houses.
Even when we do not take those into account I find that out of three million workers earning more than $1,000 a year in Canada, 2,400,000 of them earn $3,000 or less and therefore are completely out of the picture with regard to building houses under the National Housing Act. What it really amounts to, Mr. Chairman, is that this 70 per cent of new housing which is spoken of in the report of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has been built for some 10 per cent of our population.
It has been suggested that large strides have been made in overcoming the housing shortage in Canada, but that contention does not seem to be borne out by the brief which was presented by the planning board, heads of departments and officials of the municipality of metropolitan Toronto to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects, because I find in that report on the housing situation in the city of Toronto we have this statement. They point out that the existing shortage is some 25,000 units. In the period between 1955 and 1980 it is calculated they will require some 460,000 units. They have some other figures dealing with the age of the houses that are in existence which I think would probably increase the requirements for housing there. We find that many of them will be 65 years old by 1980 and the majority of them may be well over 100 years old by that time. These are units that are still considered as useful and usable housing.
The report has this interesting statement to make, too, Mr. Chairman:
Both the typical apartment units being constructed and the suburban houses appear to be available to only a relatively small segment of the total population. In 1954 median wage or salary income in the area appeared to be less than $2,900, and less than one quarter of the wage and salary earners received more than $4,000. It is doubtful that these levels have increased by more than a few per cent since then. Nevertheless, the minimum going rental for new 2 bedroom apartments in the city is around $135, and in the suburbs it is around $105; average rentals are, respectively, $150 and $120. Even allowing for multiple wage earners in many families, it is unlikely that as many as 10 per cent of the families in the area can afford to pay even the minimum going rentals for new apartment accommodation.

National Housing Act
It would appear from that, Mr. Chairman, that not only is the 70 per cent of new housing which consists of single homes confined to a very small percentage of our population, but that a very large part of our rental housing projects which have been going up is also confined to people in the same income bracket. Pointing out the situation in the Toronto area, the report says:
Nor can the majority of the area's families afford to buy single-family houses in the suburbs, which constitute the bulk of the area's supply of new housing. Minimum qualifying income for an N.H.A. loan on the cheapest sale unit which is currently available in the Toronto area-semidetached houses in Scarborough selling at $10,500- is $3,600; with a working wife in the family, the minimum qualifying income for household heads is at best $3,100 or $3,200.
I think these figures show conclusively that while the National Housing Act might have been extremely useful to the more fortunate segment of our population which is in the minority, it has been completely useless with regard to meeting the housing requirements of the vast majority of our people. One does not need to look at reports of this kind to know what the situation is, and one does not need to look outside the city of Ottawa to realize that many people are living in dwellings which are unfit for human habitation.
Mention has been made here on several occasions of the appalling record of fires in this city. It is perfectly obvious, when one reads of the districts in which they take place and when one sees the pictures of the dwellings, that these are substandard dwellings that should have been abandoned long ago. The people within them, of course, fall into the category of those in an income bracket who cannot afford either to rent decent rental accommodation or to build an N.H.A. house.
I was interested in the comment the minister made when he opened this discussion, and I hope he will correct me if I misunderstood him. I understood him to say that the act was to be widened in such a way that the federal government's contribution toward land assembly and the clearance of slum areas could perhaps be applied to an area part of which at least might be devoted to the assembly and clearance for industrial purposes. Was I correct in that?
That immediately raises the question in my mind as to what is going to become of the people now living in those areas. What provision is going to be made to provide them with some reasonable alternative for the habitations they are now in, if areas that are going to be assembled under this act are going to be taken out of housing and placed in industry? I think that is an all-important problem to be considered.

As the hon. member for Eglinton pointed out, in the Regent Park development in Toronto more people were housed than originally lived in the area. I suggest that if the policy enunciated by the minister is to be carried out and if an area is to be cleaned up at the cost of available housing accommodation, because part of the area is to be put to industrial uses, some provision will have to be made for those who may lose their accommodation. The minister shakes his head. That would seem to indicate that the area would be large enough to provide a sufficient number of apartment houses to house as many as or more than the number of people now living in the present housing units. I did not notice the minister suggesting that there is to be a limit to the amount of an area that might be devoted to industrial purposes.
While I am on this question of apartment house construction may I suggest that there is an urgent need for some supervision with regard to the type of apartment construction now going on in some of our city areas. Perhaps these apartment buildings were not built under the N.H.A., but buildings have been constructed which never should have been allowed to be constructed. I have been spending my week ends lately visiting two members of my family, one of whom lives in Toronto and the other in Montreal, both living in comparatively new apartment houses. I venture to say that those buildings are nothing short of a disgrace. In one instance the building was built only two years ago, in the other instance five years ago. The rentals being paid could be paid only by people getting at least the $4,000 per annum which has been suggested as the minimum for building under the N.H.A.
Many of these areas now being built up will degenerate into slum areas before very long. I suggest that the federal government should be taking vigorous action in conjunction with the municipalities, much more vigorous action than is suggested by the words of the resolution now before us. I suggest that perhaps we should take a leaf out of the experience they have had in Great Britain. When I was there two years ago I was much impressed by the extent to which the public authorities, both the central government and the county councils, in conjunction had embarked upon the provision of low rental housing for the people of Britain.
While admittedly much of that housing would appear to us as being hopelessly outmoded in design, this was not true of all parts of Britain. I was particularly pleased to find that in the remote parts of the west highlands of Scotland, where my ancestors came from, they had some excellent housing

projects, in some of which I stayed, which were built with a combination of county council and central government funds. If the people of Britain are able to undertake enterprises of that sort in order to take care of their people, then a much wealthier country such as Canada should not be falling behind in that regard.
I suggest that the figures we have from such organizations as the municipality of metropolitan Toronto indicate that so far the National Housing Act has not even begun to cope with the problem of housing the Canadian people. While it may be true, according to the report of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, that the Canadian people have shown an unmistakable preference for single detached houses, I suggest that for the vast majority of the Canadian people that is like having a preference to become a millionaire. It is very nice, but it is something quite beyond their reach. Experience shows that they are just not going to get it. The result is that we have to pay some attention to alternative types of housing.
I find the trend toward apartment dwelling quite unpleasant. I would not like to live in an apartment, but apparently that is to be the fate of many of our people. If that is so, then there should be some real effort made to create apartment house developments of the proper type. I have been impressed with the unfortunate position in which many young couples are placed through having to live in apartment houses in our large cities. I really do not know how they manage to raise their children, because there is only one place for the children to play; that is on the sidewalks.
I suggest that our municipalities should be encouraged and aided by the federal government on most generous terms to develop apartment house units which would provide some of the amenities that go with living in detached houses, which is the hopeless ambition of many Canadian people according to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I suppose the resolution we have before us represents one slight faltering step toward improving an act which in the last two years has been demonstrably so deplorably weak.
I should like to see the act much stronger than it is, and I would be able to vote for it with much more vigour if it were. I think this new legislation is going to fall short of doing what all reports tell us has to be done. Why the government is hanging back, I do not know. I suggest that before very long alternative fields of investment for public funds are going to be one of the major problems of this government, and I can think of no field that is more worthy of their attention and serious consideration than that

National Housing Act
which is offered by a real attempt to grapple with the housing problem of the Canadian people.
I hope we are not going to hear any more about our proud record of building houses in Canada when we are faced with facts such as those presented by the metropolitan council of Toronto, when we are faced with economic facts such as are presented by the bureau of statistics, which prove beyond any doubt that the present housing act is incapable of housing the Canadian people. It may be that we have built over 100,000 housing units, but let us see whom we have built them for, let us consider what income brackets have been affected. I am strongly of the opinion that in a matter like housing we should be starting at the bottom, we should be making sure that there will be no longer in Canada families living in the sort of houses we find right here in the city of Ottawa, houses which are so defective in construction that they result in disastrous and fatal fires. Such houses constitute a most disgraceful and broken down slum area, such as can hardly be equalled in any city in Canada.
These are the problems which this government does not seem to want to tackle. It wants to tackle the rehousing of people with fairly adequate incomes on a sound actuarial basis by guaranteeing bank loans that are going to be paid back anyway because the people have sufficient income. I suggest that we should get right back into the public housing business; we should realize that the housing of the Canadian people is the responsibility of the whole community in Canada, and we as representatives of that community should be pressing for amendments that will be wide and strong enough to accomplish that purpose.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTRIBUTIONS TO MUNICIPALITIES, HOME LOANS, HOUSING RESEARCH, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hesitated a little to rise at this time, because I said to the minister at noon that I would not say anything unless I knew what I was talking about. So I am under quite a disability here this afternoon.
I should like to repeat at this time the tribute that was paid to Mr. Mansur for the work he did as head of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, as it was echoed by the hon. member for Eglinton. As a matter of fact I should take particular pride in it, because Mr. Mansur has moved to York West and is presently engaged there in helping us along with real estate development in my own constituency. As a matter of fact his choice of York West may have been motivated by the fact-and I think the hon. member might confirm this-that we have probably as much housing going on there under the provision of his statute as anywhere in Canada.

National Housing Act
I was thinking this afternoon that there is some type of change in this house in connection with the discussion of housing; not that I have been here so long, but there was a certain degree of urgency about it in previous years, and that seems to have disappeared to a great extent. As a matter of fact I do not hand out congratulations very often on a general basis, and I can only feel that if that sense of urgency has disappeared from this house to a great extent then the minister himself should be congratulated, because he must have had a good deal to do with alleviating that previous feeling that it was most important that many things be done for housing in general. So I congratulate him in connection with the strides that have been made in housing. I feel they have been giant strides, and the figures that have been given indicate that we are going a long way toward solving this housing problem.
I should not like to go along with some of the suggestions I have heard this afternoon about rental housing. I listened to the hon. member for Nanaimo as he talked about the great public housing we need now. I think we probably do, but it seems to me that the thing of most vital importance in connection with housing is the construction of individual homes. The home is the place where the lifeblood of the nation is best fostered. As long as we have good, strong homes contained in individual housing units, to a great extent we are going to have a great and strong Canada.
When we talk about all these people who require housing, there is a group of people about whom we have been forgetting. I think they are the forgotten class. We attempt to cover the whole sphere as well as we can, but it seems to me that the people who are really feeling the pinch at the present time are the white collar workers. They are the people who seem to contribute to every fund that comes along-it does not matter what it is-to unemployment insurance, and so on, and they are also the people that do not seem to get anything out of anything. So I feel they are the people for whom we should see what we can do in connection with broadening the scope of our activities in our housing program.
We heard the hon. member for Regina City talk about doubling up. I do not think it is voluntary. It may be voluntary to the extent that a great many of the landlords are doing it voluntarily because they must have that income in order to meet the rising cost of living, which is reflected for them to a great extent in the rising municipal taxes. It is most important that we do not make that type of living compulsory if we can


possibly avoid it. Of course for the other party to the doubling up, about whom we have heard, it is compulsory from their standpoint because they cannot put together even the small amount that is required now in some instances as a down payment under the act.
So I do not think people can be considered as doubling up voluntarily. I think it is a compulsory solution for them. Believe it or not, I think it applies more to that group of salaried white collar workers who, as I say, seem to be feeling the pinch all around in connection, with the rising cost of living.
I might mention as well that I am just wondering about the question of the interest rate, which I see fluctuates a little. I think the minister's interest rate is probably tied down to the rate set by the Bank of Canada for loans to the chartered banks, and they in turn are passing it on. The same type of financing is reflected also in this particular legislation. However, there appears to be little reason for that fluctuation. I have been told it is required to be raised periodically because building materials are in short supply, and that is one way to do the job.
As long as housing is required, as it is, there seems to be little reason for a guaranteed loan to be fluctuating. I might mention that when it fluctuates upward and a man is told, "This year you are going to pay 5| per cent instead of 5 per cent, or 5J instead of 51 per cent", remember that when it is dropped down next year you do not do anything for him because even under the best mortgage legislation he would have to go five years before he could refinance and have his interest rate dropped. So when you raise it and say, "We are doing this in 1956 because certain things are in short supply", then we are penalizing that man for a minimum period of five years.
I might go further. There are other loans that are granted by the regular companies and are tied closely to the plan that is covered by this legislation. Some of them are even for 15-year periods, and you put your name on the dotted line for the whole period. If you wish to refinance, you may do so in five years; but the cost of renewal, the cost of renegotiating the loan, imposes a penalty of a raise in interest, perhaps carried on for a period of ten years, if you wanted to spread it out.
With respect to these guaranteed loans, I feel, for instance, if farmers could get an interest rate of 5 per cent, there is no reason why this type of loan should not be acceptable to the lending institutions when we once and for all set the rate at 5 per cent and saw that it stayed there. There would be no

particular penalty then on anyone for any particular year in which he might have acquired his home.
There is one thing to which I shall be referring as I go along. It is that to a great extent we are not putting up this money. It is not something we are taking right out of the federal treasury and handing around to help people. No; we are guaranteeing it. I think a few of the previous speakers have asked the minister to tell us how much we had to take out of our pockets to make up these guarantees. I should think that, with conditions as they are, this has not cost the federal treasury very much. So I do not think we can sit back smugly and say we are doing a great deal about housing and that it has cost this government a good deal of money.
When we talk about increasing the amount for home improvement loans from $125 million to $200 million, and increasing the amount of loans in respect of which insurance policies may be issued, from $2 billion to $4 billion, we are guaranteeing that much more money, but we are not paying it out of the federal treasury.
Another item that is dealt with in the resolution, which is certainly of vital importance in the area of metropolitan Toronto, is the problem of land assembly. In my opinion this is probably the place where we require the most aggressive action, because if we do not move quickly in connection with the land assembly program the land will slip through the fingers of province and dominion or municipality and dominion. The cost's will be so great that the net amount for which we may be responsible will be staggering.
If you talk to people about the cost of house construction at the present time I think you will find that by far the most important item in the fast developing urban areas is the cost of land. You even hear it said that in the case of homes costing maybe $12,000 there may be $3,000 of that amount tied up in the very small plot upon which the home is erected. Therefore if we really want to do something to promote the cause of maintaining the prices of homes at the lowest level possible, this is the direction in which we must look in order to carry out the program. I think it will be found that over the last couple of years labour costs in the construction industry have been pretty well stabilized and are not going up too rapidly. The same is true of material costs. Therefore it will be most unfortunate if the advantages of all the new developments in home construction, the new types of articles now in use that cut the cost of materials and the labour-saving devices now used in construction, are lost in a
National Housing Act
general increase in land costs. I shall probably refer to this item again in summing up.
Then there is the question of the down payment. I do not think you can have homes for nothing. I think you have to put something into a home. I think you have to have a sense of ownership. If the down payment is going to be so infinitesimal that it does not matter whether you walk out of the home the next day and say that the government can take it, then you are not going to have a very firm base for home ownership. Therefore there must be a down payment of substance that will bring about the retention of that sense of home ownership which is required in order to encourage the people who own the homes to spend time fixing up their gardens and doing all the many things that you see being done in every urban centre. You see people building their own garages, building their own driveways, putting up their own picket fences and painting them, and a person has to have a real sense of ownership to go ahead and do these things.
I think the down payment could be reduced a bit in the case of the higher priced homes, but I certainly would not' like to see the situation develop here that I have seen in United States advertisements. There the amount a person must put into a home has dropped to the point where I do not think there can be any pride left in home ownership. I think back to the time when I bought my first home and the down payment was $250. I might say that was under the original act too. But at that time that down payment represented about 10 per cent of the total cost, and there was a real feeling that you had worked hard to get something and you were going to continue to hold it.
Then there is the question of the qualifications for home ownership. We have been talking about the amount of money that must be earned, and I cannot help but think that we are going to have to take another look at the question of dual family income. It seems to me that if we do not we are making a mistake, because the dual family income is being used to buy a television set, a new refrigerator, a new combination radiophonograph. Surely if the dual family income is available and is being used to provide these amenities, we would be very much better off if it were used to provide a firm basis of ownership in a home. I suggest to the minister that he take another look at the qualification required and the restrictive type of legislation we now have with respect to including the income of a wife in connection with the down payment and the carrying charges.

National Housing Act
There is another point I should like to deal with. The resolution refers to research, and the fact that we are going to provide about $5 million for that purpose. I took a look at the amount we are going to guarantee under the legislation and it is about $4 billion. I have done some figuring, and the amount to be spent on research comes to approximately [DOT]125 per cent. I assume that includes all the contests held for architects in order to get the right types of houses designed, and that it also includes the planning for the various communities.
If there is any place we have fallen down, and fallen down badly, I think it is right there. I do not think we have made proper use of these facilities. I am concerned that in spite of the fact that contests are held and plans are designed, I can still go out and see row upon row of the same type of housing being built, I think one hon. member said that this might result in our having further blighted areas in years to come.
I would say that we should take advantage of the research personnel we have available. It seems to me that if we took full advantage of them we would be able to have communities with homes of different types of construction and possessing an individuality that would result in their continuing to have a good resale value in the future. Remember that if we fail in this respect the person who will suffer is the actual home owner.
I shall only be about two minutes more, Mr. Chairman. I could finish now; otherwise we could call it six o'clock.

I say that in that respect we have not taken full advantage of the services of architects. Giving a prize for the development of some design is a very good thing, but we should make more use of architects. It might be that it would mean the addition of a couple of hundred dollars to the price of the individual house, but if in the long run there was a retention of that value in the house I would say that would be spending money wisely. It seems to me that what is required is that when one of these communities is planned the government should take the lead in seeing to it that we do not have the same type of construction apparent everywhere.
There is one further item, the position in which our municipalities find themselves as a result of the large-scale housing developments now taking place. I hope I will be forgiven for saying this, but it seems to me that no matter what subject comes up I can


find evidence of stress in our municipalities in attempting to handle the problems created by the influx of people into the municipalities and the new buildings that are going up. I have suggested and am going to continue to suggest various means whereby we might do something for the municipalities. The other day I talked about the federal government assuming some obligation for education. It seems to me that right here is a real opportunity to do something about the problem of education costs.
There are a multiplicity of developments which are controlled almost solely by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Immediately these developments take place the question of the capital cost of the construction of educational facilities arises. Here is an opportunity for the federal government not to guarantee something but to pay for something. It seems to me that if we could assume the capital cost of the construction of educational facilities in these new areas as they came along, it would be a great step forward. The vehicle is available and we should make use of it.
If I could sum up, sir, I think I would propose a five point program for us to carry out. First of all we should fix the rate of interest at 5 per cent. It is still going to be a good loan for these institutions, and it is going to help the people who really need help. Second, I would say we should make that down payment as low as possible but still retaining that sense of ownership that is required so that everybody is going to be proud to be a home owner. Third, I would say we have to make a wider basis for calculating the income of the family. As I said before, if the dual family income can purchase things that are not as important as houses, then let us see if we cannot make some changes there.
Fourth, we should have an aggressive land policy. We are going to have to go far afield to get land, and we are going to have to do it quickly or it is going to be too late. It is going to cost too much. We should, as soon as possible, set aside the land that is going to be needed for urban areas. Lastly, we should provide some real relief for the municipalities by taking those areas in which Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is going to develop communities and seeing that land is set aside for school facilities. Let us see if we cannot assume the capital cost of construction of these schools.
Someone will say that is going to interfere with provincial rights. We can make grants, and the municipalities can retain control. In this way they could get these schools which they so badly need.

Thank you for allowing me to speak after six.
