speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I followed the debate with a good deal of interest this afternoon. I was very glad when the hon. member for Eglinton was able to take some time to describe the very interesting project which has been completed in Toronto. I think it is a great pity that more hon. members cannot boast of similar projects all across the country.
My interest in this subject goes back some years. I find that my first speech on housing was made back in 1942, but on June 21, 1943, I referred to the picture that was being presented to the world by such well-known people as President Roosevelt of the United States as he described the slums which had existed in his country for many years. He said, as I quoted him at page 3844 of Hansard of June 21, 1943:
The program of clearing slums and providing decent homes for the ill-housed of our nation in the years before the war laid the foundation for the intensified housing effort necessary today. The job of clearing the slums, which your conference helped to begin, of necessity must be reduced substantially for the duration. With the scarcity of building materials we can now afford to build homes only in defence areas. But the goal of a slumless America must be preserved.
The hon. member for York West stressed the fact that most Canadians would like to have their own homes and gardens, and there is no quarrel with that; but the hon. member for Nanaimo pointed out correctly that the great majority of the Canadian people just are not going to have the good fortune to have their own homes or their own gardens unless the governments-and I say "governments" because municipal and provincial governments as well as the federal government must face this problem-take more interest in the problem of housing. Unless governments take more interest in the problem of housing a very large number of our citizens are condemned to spend most of a lifetime in dangerous housing quarters in the crowded attics of our cities.
I remember when Mr. Nash, who was then the minister of finance in New Zealand, visited Ottawa early in the war. He captured our imagination with two challenges. One was to the effect that everyone in New Zealand who joined the services would find himself when the war was over no worse off financially
National Housing Act
because he joined, and those who remained at home would find that they would be no better off financially because they remained at home. He also said then it was their goal to see that in New Zealand every family had a home and every citizen had a room which he could call his own, where he could close the door and say, "This is my room".
I am sorry we have not made greater progress in Canada in reaching that sort of set-up. I am sorry the Minister of Public Works is not more ambitious. I understand that he has no special desire to be the prime minister of this country. I think that is a great pity. If he had that sort of ambition I am sure he would be doing a much more imaginative job than he is doing, because I can think of no single thing that a minister of the crown could do than really tackle the problem of rural and urban housing in Canada, harness our great resources toward the clearing away of slums and the providing of the type of housing which we can expect from our lumber and other resources which are here in such generous supply.
The hon. member for York West was about to launch a very eloquent appeal, I thought he was going to say, on behalf of the neglected group in our economy. I was all ready to shed tears for the old age pensioners because I thought that was the group he had in mind, but he went on to discuss the white collar group, a group that probably does not need a great deal of sympathy in this particular set-up.
While I think we are all happy that a large volume of better houses is being built in Canada I think on the whole those who are taking advantage of the facilities the minister provides would have been able to provide better housing on their own. I know they would have had to pay higher interest charges; they would have had to make higher down payments, but they would have had better housing. They would have had less money available for television sets or new cars or some of the other very desirable things that people want and do have nowadays. By and large those who have been able to take advantage of the facilities we have do not require a great deal of sympathy, but the large sector of our people who are not earning or are not receiving enough to qualify for loans under the legislation do require our sympathy.
I am sure many hon. members have read "Fourteen days as an old age pensioner" by William MacEachern, reprinted from the Toronto Daily Star. I suggest that the Minister of Public Works, since he is a public-spirited citizen, might take a couple of weeks sometime and just see how easy it is to get desirable living quarters on the sort of money

National Housing Act
that an old age pensioner has. This young chap took $20, half a month's pension, and then proceeded to find the sort of quarters he could obtain. In this paragraph he describes the place he finally settled on. It happened to be a $5 a week proposition. He said:
The room was in an old, tired-looking bungalow in the Broadview-Queen district. It smelled like an old maid's trunk-the pungent, hygienic smell of mothballs, but it was a clean smell. The room was clean, too, although it looked cold and unlived-in. There were old lace curtains on the window and a frayed rug on the floor.
I knew I couldn't do much better for $5, but I thought I'd better look around a bit before I took it. I told the owner-his name was Tommy and he was an old age pensioner, too ("I'm 72", he said, but he didn't look any more than 50) 

that I thought my grandfather would like it and I would bring him down tomorrow and help him move in.
The young chap said he was negotiating on behalf of his grandfather. With respect to the $6 a week room he had this to say:
The $6 place was on Parliament street, above a jam factory. A sickening, clammy smell of warm jam hung in the air. I followed the owner up a stairway into a darkened hallway. He gave a light switch a few fast clicks. "Guess it doesn't work", he said. "We'll have to get that fixed". (The same routine was repeated a dozen times before the day was over).
The room was dark and dingy; one lonely bulb hung from the ceiling and the only window was so small you could look out of it only one eye at a time.
The room looked big because it hadn't any furniture-just a table and an ashtray. "We'll put a bed in here for him," the man said. "We can dig one out of the pile in there". He pointed to a store room across the hall where broken chairs, ruptured mattresses and other iron and wooden stuff was stacked in a wild heap.
Then he described the worst place he visited. He said:
The worst place of all was on Dundas street. Here I had to pass through a pitch-black hallway, through a room piled high with boxes, pots and pans, old stoves, broken-down iceboxes, through another hallway and down a ladder. We weaved around several water tanks and furnaces, ducked under a network of dripping pipes, and into a low-ceilinged, windowless dungeon. The "room" was cold and damp and there was sweat on the concrete walls.
There was no radiator, just a battered-up electric affair. The bed was mussed and the sheets looked mouldy.
The owner said he wanted $7, and I shuddered. I wouldn't live there if he paid me $5. What would I do if a fire broke out?
Then he described some of the places that were available in Toronto, the only possible living quarters that anyone whose limit was $40 a month could expect to find. I am sure no one in this chamber is very proud of the fact that a large sector of the Canadian people are sentenced to live most of their lives in the sort of quarters described so vividly in "Fourteen days as an old age pensioner".

In the same city, in "Toronto the good", you read a very different story. In Maclean's magazine Toronto is described as the world's fastest growing city. I am referring to this, Mr. Chairman, because I think the government has waited far too long in taking the sort of action that must be taken in connection with land assembly questions to prevent the kind of thing that is happening.
The story in Maclean's of March 17, 1956, entiled "The fastest growing city in the world" tells about a woman named Sarah Palk who had some land that had been in the family for about 70 years. It had been bought for a few cents an acre a good many years ago. It was sold at what seemed to be a very high price, $145,000. The buyer then added another $50,000 to the price and sold it for $195,000. The next buyer was not satisfied with peanuts and he turned it over for $355,000.
In view of that type of speculation in connection with property and housing it is small wonder that many people find themselves obliged to pay fantastic prices for property. The piece of property I have just referred to increased in price from $145,000 to $355,000 within a short space of time.
This article also tells about one of the shrewdest real estate people in Toronto who a short time ago offered for sale a piece of property for $70,000. After his death it was sold for $250,000. I do not think anyone can argue that this type of turnover or profit has been achieved as a result of the sweat and tears of any individual. Many of these larger centres have attracted speculators who have added fantastic, fictitious and exorbitant prices to the real value of property.
I have knowledge of a deal involving friends of mine in the Hamilton area which took place just before Easter. This involves a new house that had been built on property which had been farm land three years ago. I do not know what price the farmer received for the land, but my friends paid $3,500 for quite a small lot, scarcely large enough for a vegetable and flower garden. They paid $3,500 for a small piece of farm land on which their house was built, which means an enormous capital gain on the part of some speculator.
When I spoke about housing during the war years I was able to refer to the fact that in countries like Holland, Sweden and Denmark they took the necessary precautions 100 years ago to ensure that speculation did not enter into and increase the cost of housing. I think it is a great pity that the minister has not used more imagination and given greater leadership in an effort to halt developments such as those described in

Maclean's of March 17. I think it is correct to say that these conditions apply to every major city in Canada.
At the time I visited my friends in Hamilton I also visited some farm friends in Ontario who are feeling the impact of this type of development. A gentleman who sold a farm for $150,000 for a subdivision along the Queen Elizabeth highway moved back from that area and offered a young couple $65,000 for a farm which they had bought just a few years ago for approximately $20,000. It is very disturbing for young people who are trying to earn an honest living producing food for the nation to have these speculative offers made to them. Someone who knew something about the increase in land value in the Toronto area and who was interested in making some money in a few years would be able to anticipate that the farm which sold for $65,000 today might well be worth two or three hundred thousand dollars a few years later.
I submit that this is having a very disturbing effect on our economy. Within a few miles of nearly every rapidly growing city in Canada a fantastic increase is taking place in the valuation of land. This in turn is passed on to the house builders, and presents a real hardship to them as they try to meet the increased cost of insurance and of servicing property out of their limited earnings.
The minister told us something about the achievements which have been made in the field of new housing. I am very glad that an increasing number of Canadian people are able to look forward to having new houses. This will result in their vacating houses which will be made available to other people with lower incomes.
Over the supper hour I again looked at the figures for the distribution of non-farm income in Canada. I find that the median income

which means that half the people get less than this figure and half the people get more-by provinces is as follows: Atlantic provinces, $2,089; Quebec, $2,730; Ontario, $3,109; prairie provinces, $2,395 and British Columbia, $2,759. In view of the incomes I have quoted the minister will realize that well over half the people in Canada can never hope to take advantage of the housing facilities that are available.
I think one would not need much of an imagination to agree with the hon. member for Eglinton when he was discussing the costs involved in the new housing project in Toronto, particularly when you take into consideration the costs in that area for juvenile delinquency, tuberculosis and fire hazards. I feel sure that anyone who is in Toronto 50
National Housing Act
years from now will be able to demonstrate quite clearly that the people of our day made a sound investment in clearing away slums and providing desirable quarters for an increased number of people who are now living in the Regent Park area.
Just yesterday I visited Iroquois and saw what has been done there in the way of building a new community. There is nothing especially spectacular there, but they are allowing more ground for construction. I noticed that every house in the new town of Iroquois is going to have a chimney from the basement to above roof level. I am sure this one innovation in building practices in that community will result in an almost total elimination of fires in the Iroquois area.
When you take into consideration the loss of life in Ottawa through fires, it seems a great pity that the minister along with the civic and provincial authorities cannot proceed with the establishing of slum clearing projects in the capital city so that when people come here, as they do, from all over the world the minister will be able to demonstrate to them what has been accomplished as the result of co-operation among the three levels of government.
In terms of providing a stimulus to business I think it will be readily agreed that housing in Canada is a field wherein we can provide employment. Here is a way in which employment can be provided for the lumbering industry and the plumbing and building supplies people. Only 56 per cent of rural homes have electricity; 75 per cent of rural nonfarm homes have electricity, while 99 per cent of urban homes have this convenience. When it comes to running water, only 32 per cent of farm homes and 46 of non-farm homes have this convenience. Then when we come to the question of installed bath or# shower, telephone, mechanical refrigeration and so on, the statistics as to the use of these necessary conveniences, at least in the opinion of most Canadians, would suggest that here is a field where the minister could provide assured employment for a large number of Canadians for many years to come.
It will hardly be during the time of the minister as a minister of the crown that the housing problems of Canada will be solved and the goal which President Roosevelt mentioned back in 1943 realized. A slumless America is not likely to be realized during the minister's time unless we make a great deal more progress in the next ten years than we have in the last ten years.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks in support of this resolution will be brief and will be confined to the National Housing Act in so far as it applies to the Yukon Territory. The rising number of applications for

National Housing Act
loans clearly demonstrates the effectiveness and success of the legislation as it applies to the more populated areas of Canada. In the Yukon and other places in northern Canada it is a different story, but one which can and should be remedied at once.
The government has indicated its intention to encourage and co-operate in various ways in the development of the Yukon Territory, and has specifically indicated its intention to develop the Yukon Territory by the encouragement of home building and home ownership in the new subdivision planned for the east side of the Yukon river adjacent to the city of Whitehorse. The cost of building dwellings in the Yukon exceeds the cost of building similar or like dwellings in any other portion of Canada save the Northwest Territories.
Recently I discussed this problem with an official of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, with regard to the application of the National Housing Act to the Yukon, particularly in view of the prevailing construction costs, and urged that an adjustment in the appraisal be made to recognize the cost of construction in that area and to be in line with representations of the Whitehorse board of trade and other interested organizations and individuals.
I find that during the fall of 1955 cost surveys were conducted throughout Canada by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and from the results of this survey new appraisal rates were computed. I understand that those new appraisal rates were put into effect just prior to the end of 1955. My understanding is that the basic appraisal rate which is now in use for the city of Whitehorse will in the majority of cases result in loans to applicants equal to the maximum loans allowable under the legislation.
As you know, the National Housing Act limits the allowable maximum loan on any dwelling in relation to the square footage of the unit, with an over-all allowable maximum of $12,800. For instance, a 1,000 square jfoot frame bungalow built according to standard specifications in Whitehorse would qualify under the legislation for a maximum loan of $10,250, plus the insurance fee of 2 per cent. The appraisal of the unit may provide for a larger loan, but the amount allowable would be limited to $10,250.
The act requires that the gross debt service ratio in respect to the home owner or home purchaser should not exceed 23 per cent of the gross income of the home owner or purchaser. In some circumstances the approved lender may with the concurrence of the corporation approve a borrower where this ratio

is exceeded. Therefore the income of the borrower has a direct bearing on the amount of loan possible.
I want to point out that living costs in the Yukon range from 30 to 50 per cent higher than outside, and by that I mean the more populated areas in the provinces, while building costs are from 40 per cent to 50 per cent higher. Only a modest home can be built in Canada for $10,000 and by the same token $15,000 is required to construct a comparatively modest home in Whitehorse. Add to this the cost of a lot at say $1,500 and you are left with a $16,500 expenditure. I can assure you that this will not provide lavish accommodation.
The obvious remedy should not be too difficult, and that is to have the valuation on which the loan will be calculated based on Whitehorse prices. This would automatically give a maximum loan of $12,800 to anyone building, let us say, a $15,000 home. I believe I can best illustrate this point by quoting an editorial which appeared in the Whitehorse Star, which reads:
Peering from the deep shadows of tar paper shacks and old log cabins-and from well-built homes too-is a large population of would-be housebuilders. Many have a thousand dollars or so socked away in the bank, careful dollar piled on careful dollar, which they hope will serve some day as down payment on a clean, bright and cheerful home for themselves and for their families. But, alas for these northern citizens, most of them may be denied the early benefits of government assisted construction under N.H.A. terms. Reason for roadblock in the path of their wishes is the application of figures based on outside construction costs to Yukon N.H.A. loans. Using these standards, houses rise like fireweed outside, fertilized by the reasonable down payments of ordinary citizens but, in the Yukon, where builders quote costs as much as 40 per cent higher than outside, ciitzens in similar circumstances to their outside cousins cannot raise the necessary cash for the initial payment-or will be able to do so only after years of saving.
Here's how it works: the lending value for a house and lot (in other words the amount of money at which N.H.A. assesses lot and building planned by the would-be borrower) say the authorities, "Will be a reasonable cost of building the house plus a reasonable cost for the land."
Unfortunately this "reasonable" cost means reasonable outside cost. Maximum loan value is calculated at 90 per cent of the first $8,000 of the lending value and 70 per cent of the balance In the case of a single house. Maximum loan for a single house is $12,800.
For instance, on a lending value of $10,000 a down payment of $1,400 would be required. For a $12,000 house, $2,000 would be required. But loans are also controlled on a square foot basis. Under this arrangement, the maximum loan available for a house containing floor space of 750 square feet is $8,000 and for each square foot in excess of 750 the loan may be increased by $9 a square foot up to $12,800.
This is where the trouble lies for the Yukoner. Take as an example the 750-square-foot, by no means lavish house that might be built outside for $8,000. Cost of this in Whitehorse, figured at

40 per cent higher than outside, would be $11,200. However, under N.H.A., there is no provision for this increased cost. The Yukon man-of-the-house must pay the difference himself. On this $8,000 house, as approved by present N.H.A. standards, he will be required to put up a down payment of $800. In addition he will be required to pay the difference between $8,000 and $11,200 which is $3,200, making a total of $4,000 from the family bank account before work can be started on the house. Hard times indeed.
What is being sought under leadership of the board of trade is not an increase in maximum loan available ($12,800) but an increase, for the Yukon, in assessment of lending values. A house is going to cost more here than outside so why not adjust lending values to suit Yukon costs, That is, permit the would-be homeowner to borrow up to the real cost of the house he plans to build here, not force him to borrow on the basis of building a similar home outside.
We hear frequently from government sources the word that "Canada's eyes are on the north." If this is so then there is no reason why there should be a lowering of N.H.A. eyes when it comes to Yukon home-building. Homes are the foundation upon which orderly northern development must be built from here on in.
It has been found that inspectors from Alberta are prone to evaluate dwellings constructed in the Yukon in accordance with the price structure and cost of building in the province of Alberta, which price structure and cost of building is approximately 40 to 50 per cent lower than the price structure and cost of building in the Yukon.
Last month a senior head office official of the corporation and the regional supervisor from the west coast visited Whitehorse. At that time meetings were held with representatives of the city and other interested organizations to explain the operations of the National Housing Act. No doubt the corporation now realizes the problem with which the people of the Yukon are faced, and it is to be hoped that their recommendations for amendments to the act or regulations will be in line with existing conditions; otherwise the building of dwellings will be seriously curtailed if not rendered entirely impossible.
I am sure all hon. members heartily agree that Yukoners should not be penalized to this extent when a few minor amendments to the act or regulations could easily rectify the existing situation. I am sure the minister is sympathetic to the cause and will find some solution to the problem.

think all levels of society in Canada, and most of the people of Canada, are prepared to admit that the need of individuals to own their own homes is very basic in our society. To the extent that it is met, to the extent that we can make home ownership available to more and more people, we establish a stable base to our society and, to some extent at least, a shelter from whatever adverse conditions the community may encounter.
National Housing Act
When we think in terms of home ownership, we think almost always in terms of the little plot of ground and the single house unit, and that is a very necessary concept. But those of us in the larger cities, and perhaps particularly in the city of Montreal and the province of Quebec, are very conscious too of the need not for individual unit housing development, but for the construction of apartment units and consolidated units which contain accommodation for many families.
We are particularly conscious-and this will be the tenor of my short remarks tonight -of the need for rehabilitation of our rundown areas. I often wonder whether people generally have any idea of the living conditions in a genuine slum area, the sort of area where, whether you go into it by day or by night, as one city councillor in Montreal phrased it last week, you see two-legged rats and four-legged rats. The four-legged ones, of course, are those that are familiar to us all. The two-legged ones would perhaps have been decent, honest and helpful human beings had it not been for the warping of their characters, the crimes they have committed and the back alleys down which they have been led as a result of the circumstances under which they live.
One could go on and outline the conditions in slum areas, but it is hardly necessary. However, we should remember that one of the main reasons for the development of these slum areas has been the natural desire of a large section of our population to live close to their places of work. That is particularly so in the large cities, where transportation difficulties are quite a problem, where it is becoming, indeed, quite a costly business just to get from your home to your place of work if you have to go by a mass transport system of any kind whatsoever.
These people do not want to be moved from the area in which they are located. It is true that they would like to have better housing, but apparently they are prepared to stay there even at the very great inconvenience of the type of accommodation with which they have to put up. In Montreal, for example, just recently there was a survey in one of the most run-down slum areas of the city. To the amazement of everybody who was there-because one tends to think of everybody as wanting to move out of the centre of the city and into little houses on the outside-83-7 per cent of the people in that area wanted to be relocated there, in terms of a new housing development, a new slum clearance project that was then under consideration. Eighty-four per cent, practically the entire bulk of the population, wanted to stay right there where they were

National Housing Act
close to their work, where they were close to the centre of the city, where the facilities they knew so well, their churches, their stores, their schools and so on could all continue to be available to them.
That, to my mind, puts a tremendous emphasis upon one aspect of this legislation which is to come before us, and that is that it should fully provide for slum clearance and the redevelopment of slum areas in the major cities of this country. I know there has been considerable activity in that connection under the existing act, and I think it has been welcomed by all of us. It is well to remember, however, that in the case of this particular project in Montreal, which seems to be coming to fruition quite rapidly, the cost of acquiring the land itself is going to be between $4 million and $5 million for this one single project, and there are 13 of these projects all equally necessary in that one city. Montreal, of course, is the oldest city in the country.
What?

It is
the oldest major city in the country. I shall correct myself in deference to the gentlemen who come from cities of great antiquity but perhaps not quite so large. Montreal is the largest city in Canada which is also of great age. It has a vested interest, almost, in slum clearance. I think that is why so many of us will follow the development of this bill, in order to see that it does contain provision to meet some of the problems that face our municipality.
I return to this question of slums and slum clearance. Slums are not just run-down housing areas. It is unfortunate that so many people think of them in that connection, and feel that money spent on slum clearance and on the redevelopment of a housing area, on building good houses in what is now a slum, is not spent too profitably. That is the attitude of a great many people. They forget that the slum is a tremendous financial drain on the entire community. I was interested last year to read a lengthy editorial in the Montreal Gazette of March 14, 1955, from which I will select only one paragraph pointing up this particular fact. Speaking of this slum area in Montreal which is to be redeveloped it had this to say:
The cost to the city of such an area-and the more alarming cost in terms of human suffering- is immense. Juvenile delinquency in the area is nine times higher than in the city as a whole. Crime among adults and complaints of all kinds are also strikingly higher. And the cost in human lives may be looked at in another way. The streets in this area are so narrow for the traffic that moves through them that the accident rate is three times higher than for the city as a whole.

Here is a representative slum area. Juvenile delinquency is nine times higher than the average for the city. Traffic accidents are three times higher. From there you can go on to add other things such as the disorganization of a family when it is forced to go into one or two rooms as housing for the father, mother and three or four children. It is a breeding ground of prostitution, gambling and all sorts of crime.
One rather striking illustration is found in another comment on this situation made by the Montreal board of trade. It refers to the slum area as "the training ground of the first offender" and goes on to say:
The costs to the community of bad housing and the slum are tangible and measurable. The effects, in ill health, discouragement, neurosis, and stunted mental and physical growth, cannot be aggregated in any statistical sense. But beyond this, the slum is a direct financial burden upon the city. On the one hand, expenditures on public health and hospitals, social agencies, police services, reformatories, jails, fire prevention, and mental institutions, are greatest for the population of bad housing areas; on the other, the share of tax revenues which such areas contribute to the city is disproportionately small. It costs governments, and society generally, more to maintain slum areas than any other parts of the city.
Then they go on to refer to a report made by the metropolitan housing authority of Cleveland before 1935, and it is interesting that with respect to the statistics compiled in Cleveland they say:
The operating loss sustained by the city, county and welfare agencies concerned, for an area 20 blocks by three blocks in size, and housing 22,236 persons, was $2 million, even without allowing for taxes unpaid during the year. For the city alone, the taxable value of the area was $10-12 per capita as compared with a cost liability of $51-10 per capita.
In other words, we see that the slum area is one of' the most costly burdens on any municipal administration today. I think we in Montreal have good reason at the present time to appreciate some of what has been accomplished by the operation of this particular legislation. After a great deal of backing, twisting and turning a preliminary report was prepared by a committee under the chairmanship of Paul Dozois of our executive committee and sparked by a very remarkable woman, Mrs. R. G. Gilbride. We then had another look at the matter. We re-examined it with the help of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and I think a great deal of credit is due to their representative in Montreal, Mr. F. F. Field.
We then had another municipal committee on the matter headed by the city councillor Mr. John Sullivan, and just last week city council decided to authorize going ahead with this particular project. But that is only one of 13 that are vitally necessary in the

city of Montreal, and I know that not only those of us in the house but the citizens of Montreal are waiting for the details of the bill. The resolution is rather broad and vague in its generalities, as is perhaps necessary, and we will be waiting for the details of the bill in order to make quite sure that it is going to enable the municipalities of this country to carry out their slum clearance projects and the development of decent housing conditions so badly needed at the present time for the majority of our citizens in these run-down areas.
I ran across a quotation this afternoon that I think is particularly pertinent to the history of this type of legislation in the house. I hope that perhaps it will spur the minister on to greater effort. It is a quotation from a speech made by a rather famous Canadian, Edward Blake, at Aurora in 1874. At that time he said:
It is the function of ministers-we know it and I do not quarrel with it-to say nothing that can be caught hold of, nothing in advance of the popular opinion of the day, to watch the current of that opinion, and when it has gathered strength, to crystallize it into acts of parliament.
As far as I have been able to see, Mr. Chairman, even though the steps taken to date have been in the right direction the housing legislation of the government has been at least one step behind and very often more than one step behind what was necessary for the development of our country and the provision of the housing facilities that we badly needed. It has been a case of crystallizing something into an act of parliament after the need had become so evident that it could not be avoided.
I would simply express my final hope that when the bill comes down it will be a forwardlooking piece of legislation that will cover not only our immediate requirements but will make some provision for our needs for a good many years to come.

To understand the situation we must understand that the city of Vancouver has reached the ultimate under its own resources as far as housing is concerned, and so has the city of New Westminster to the east of my riding. Therefore my people have the only land available for housing in the lower mainland of British Columbia.

As the hon. member for Mackenzie said today, the contractors are not trying to get big profits. The point I want to bring to the minister's attention is the fact that the contractor who wishes to build 10 or 25 homes, who owns the land and sells it to people who want to build homes, is in a very different position. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is stopping him from building homes. Mr. Pickersgill, who is the director in Vancouver, is a very fine gentleman and co-operates to the full. He must work under instructions from Ottawa, however. I know of no civil servant who will co-operate with the municipalities as well as Mr. Pickersgill does. I have no complaint against him. The minister is putting the man who is building 21 homes in the same category as these people who are developing large subdivisions, and that cannot be done. It is true that there are too many septic tanks in Burnaby. I admit that; and there

The few remarks I have to make will deal with loans from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for housing for the senior citizens of this country. I hope after listening to the very sad stories that were told by the hon. member for Mackenzie, the minister will be so conditioned now that he will listen to what I have to say. I think it goes without saying that there is a tremendous need in this country for housing projects to take care of our senior citizens. While these projects fall mainly into three categories, it is with only two of these categories I wish to deal this evening, and one in particular.
Apparently the government, through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, is not prepared to make loans on institutional types of buildings for our senior citizens. I am not too well disposed toward that type of building myself. I do not think it adds much to the welfare of our senior citizens in their later days. 1 believe the best projects which are being sponsored by Central Mortgage and Housing through these loans are the self-contained units and the hostels in connection therewith. These projects are very commendable. Certainly, the terms and conditions under which these loans are granted are very generous.
At the same time, it seems to me there are places where this institutional type of building might be a necessity. In those cases it is difficult for me to understand why the government will not make loans to limited dividend companies who want to construct buildings of that type. After all the provincial government concerned must underwrite the mortgage, and in addition the senior citizens who occupy these buildings pay rent for the space they occupy. It is rather difficult, therefore, for me to understand why the government is so averse to making these loans through Central Mortgage and Housing on these institutional type buildings.
As I said a moment ago, the government is prepared to lend money for the erection of self-contained units where such projects are sponsored by municipalities which set up limited dividend companies for that purpose. These self-contained units are for aged married couples within the community. I think it is a wonderful idea, for it enables a couple in advanced years to move into such quarters in the community in which they have spent the greater part of their lives.
IMr. Goode.]
At the same time it is rather difficult for me to understand why the government is not prepared to advance money on the hostel type of building for single aged men and women. Certainly I can understand that it would involve a considerably greater sum of money. However, as I said the provincial government concerned underwrites that obligation to Central Mortgage and Housing. I cannot see why there should be discrimination against the aged single people of this country. I should like the minister, when he speaks on this resolution, to make some comment on that aspect of the matter.
I said there was a great need for housing of this type. While I have not the statistics for all the provinces I do have a few statistics with regard to the position in Saskatchewan. I imagine the statistics for other provinces are quite comparable. In Saskatchewan the percentage of persons 65 years and over, in relation to the total population of the province, is 9 per cent or approximately 74,000. Of those 74,000 there are 24,243 in receipt of welfare assistance, and there are a few 70 and older who are getting the old age security supplementary allowance. In other words, 34 per cent of Saskatchewan's citizens of 65 years or older are in receipt of welfare assistance. Of the 24,000 some odd in receipt of extra assistance than is normally provided under old age assistance, 40 per cent are single persons. It is rather difficult, therefore, for me to understand why the government has not seen fit to make loans for buildings to house this particular category of aged citizens.
As I said a moment ago, the terms and conditions for loans on self-contained units are adequate. As a matter of fact I think they are very generous. In my own province this is the situation. The government will provide 20 per cent of the cost as an outright grant to any organization that wants to set up a limited dividend company to undertake such a project. Then Central Mortgage and Housing will make a loan for 80 per cent of the remainder. I think that is correct.
Ninety per cent.

Ninety per cent of the remainder at 3| per cent interest for a period of 40 years. Certainly nobody can question the generosity of those terms. One would think that at once there would be a great deal of interest in such a proposition when there is such a need for housing projects of this nature throughout the country. Yet what do we find? We find that, in spite of those very generous conditions, organizations and communities are not taking advantage of them as I am sure the minister and all of

us would like to see them do. As a matter of fact, in Saskatchewan in 1954 there were only 14 such projects undertaken, and some of those were undertaken without benefit of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation loan for a very specific reason. After all, it is not too logical or feasible to build a self-contained housing project in which you are going to place aged married couples in the community if you are not going to make adequate provision for the remaining consort when death separates a couple.
The government is prepared to authorize the building of hostel type buildings in conjunction with those self-contained units, but the regulations are quite limited, and it is because of those limitations that organizations and communities have not been too anxious to take advantage of the loans that are made through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Yet in the province of Saskatchewan during the last year or two, because of some misunderstanding, because of some misinterpretation of the act, and quite honestly I think, the government was prepared to permit them to go ahead on the understanding that the province originally had of this section of the act, namely that as far as the hostel type of accommodation was concerned, it was widened, and the province of Saskatchewan is now authorized until the end of June this year to allow for greater accommodation in the hostel type of building in conjunction with self-contained units.
Because of that, in the province of Saskatchewan some 30 of those projects are well under way as against 14 in 1954. I am sure that if these same conditions applied in other provinces of this country there would be a great deal more interest in this type of housing for our senior citizens. Therefore I would ask the minister to give the greatest possible consideration to allowing communities to build hostel type accommodation in connection with these other self-contained units, so that half the so-called hostel type accommodation would be occupied by two single persons and the remainder, which under the act must now be left vacant in the event of the death of one of the aged couples in the self-contained unit, be used in this way. Let the community place single aged persons in the remaining space on the understanding that they would vacate that space when one of the remaining consorts from the self-contained units had to be looked after.
In the province of Saskatchewan we have a great deal of interest because of the existing conditions as they apply in that province. I would suggest that they should apply in every other part of Canada, and I would ask
National Housing Act
the minister to give the most serious consideration to incorporating those changes into the act as soon as possible.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

Mr. Chairman, there are perhaps one or two comments I should make before the resolution does carry. At the outset I would like to thank hon. members, particularly the hon. member for Eglinton and the hon. member for York West, for their kind remarks about Mr. Mansur, who did a magnificent job in setting up Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and running it for the better part of nine years, and by so doing rendering a great public service. At the same time I wish to pay my compliments to his successor, Mr. Bates, who in the 18 months or so that he has been president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has already shown that ability which made him so effective as a deputy minister of fisheries. I am quite confident that as time develops he too will make a greater contribution to the public service of Canada.
I also wish to thank hon. members for the constructive nature of the debate today on housing. I am quite sure it reflects to the country at large that all hon. members are interested in and acutely conscious of this very important problem.
The hon. member for Eglinton, as usual, expressed some very good points. He asked the question as to whether or not the action taken by the government recently in increasing the interest rate by one-quarter of one per cent means that the government is trying to discourage housing by taking the same steps that we were obliged to take at the time of the Korean conflict. The answer to that is no. This move cannot in any way be construed as such, and certainly that was the furthest thought from our minds at that time. The interest rate that must be set is the one that will attract sufficient mortgage money to the market to enable us to achieve a good level of housing.
As the hon. member knows, this year is likely to be the greatest year in Canada's history in terms of capital expenditures and demands for money. There were indications that the supply of mortgage money from the banks and lending institutions was slowing down. It was thought it might dry up; and it became necessary, in the light of rising interest rates, to increase our interest rate to 5J per cent, which is what it was established at in the first instance in 1954.
It has always been the practice of the government to try to achieve the lowest interest rate possible in the interests of the borrower and still attract enough money to

National Housing Act
the market to achieve a high level of housing. I think the hon. member for Eglinton will recall that when we set the interest rate in the first instance it was a period when rates were declining. We waited in order to obtain the lowest possible rate, and I think perhaps he was surprised that we were able to establish a rate of 5J per cent at a time when many people thought it would be somewhat higher.
Then he mentioned Regent Park North and compared it with the development of Regent Park South, and used it to criticize what he said was a growing trend toward bureaucracy in the operations of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Regent Park North was the first and the largest slum clearance project undertaken in Canada. It was undertaken in the heart of Toronto, in a place that lent itself admirably to a slum clearance project. That was before the federal-provincial approach was developed. The result was that the municipality, with the help of the provincial government, built the housing on land acquired and cleared jointly by the municipality and the federal government. The federal government advanced a total of about $1,300,000, which represented half the cost of acquiring and clearing the land. The provincial government at that time put about $1,000 into each unit for a total of 1,289 units, and their contribution was therefore just about the same as the federal government's contribution. There was close co-operation between the housing authority and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation at that time in setting up the scales of rentals and their relationship to income. I am sure the hon. member is aware of the close co-operation that did prevail with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation at that time.
The hon. member then used that as something of a standard to compare adversely the development of Regent Park South in which Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is more directly involved through the medium of section 36 of the National Housing Act. There again Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will pay half the cost of acquiring and clearing the land. They will pay 75 per cent of the cost of completing the housing project of some 750 units on the cleared land, and will then pay 75 per cent of the net deficits or the subsidies involved.
That project has been developed under the guidance of a committee composed of representatives of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the provincial government and the municipality of metropolitan

Toronto. On the committee has been Mr. Dearlove who is the man to whom my hon. friend referred this afternoon in such deservedly warm terms-
But his recommendations have not been adopted in connection with the Regent Park South project.
Perhaps not in toto, but his advice and guidance were valued and I am sure that much of it was used.

I am well aware that Mr. Dearlove was a member of the committee to which the minister has referred, but the views of Mr. Dearlove on the various matters I discussed this afternoon were not adopted by the committee, and I think it is unfortunate that more weight was not attached to his views in the light of his experience and success in the operation of the Regent Park North project.

May I ask if the loan was approved on the basis of 90 per cent of the original tender or on the basis of 90 per cent of the eventual cost? The minister will recall that there was a difference. The first tender was the one approved by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for its 90 per cent contribution, but subsequently that tender had to be set aside and the eventual cost will be greater. Is Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation prepared to contribute 90 per cent of the higher cost?

On that particular point, Mr. Chairman, I do not have the answer now. It has been approved by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation but I have not seen it recently. I shall look at that particular aspect of it. I would like to assure the hon. member that such differences as appear to exist at this time in the approach to these two different projects, Regent Park North and Regent Park South, will be ironed out as we go along.
The hon. member said that in the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation there is developing a bureaucracy which has almost advanced to a state of autocracy. I can say to my hon. friend in the same spirit in which he said Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has become more bureaucratic, that it is not becoming more bureaucratic. Every effort is being made, in fact, to obtain the views and opinions of people and to get as close as possible to the people whom Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is trying to serve.
I think one evidence of that is the local housing authorities with local management. Another is the close relationship that obtains between Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the housebuilders' association of Canada. That relationship has been fostered
National Housing Act
through the establishment of liaison committees which operate on a district basis, and which also have access to the head office of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation on the personal invitation of the president. There is the community planning association with which the closest co-operation obtains. There has been an advisory panel set up to advise on the training of planners. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation endeavours to obtain the advice of the people it serves and to get as close as possible to them.
My hon. friend from Regina City who I must say gave a very good speech, again within the confines of socialist philosophy, dwelt, as I thought he would, on the need for houses for people of low incomes. I think that is a pretty valid position for him to take. I would say in reply that in 1955, for example, there were 132,000 new housing units completed in Canada including conversions, against family formations of something of the order of 80,000, which means there has been a gain on the backlog of over 50,000 units. When you couple that with the fact that there is nobody in Canada who is not housed in accommodation of some sort or other, it can be seen that the movement to the new houses has left a great many houses vacant which do come into the possession of the class of people the hon. member for Regina had in mind when he spoke.
In addition to that there is the expansion of the home improvement sections of the act which are contemplated by this resolution. They give people in this salary group an opportunity to improve their homes and thereby improve their accommodation.
Would the minister then suggest that the government's policy is to allow this trickling-down process to take care of the housing needs of people in the low income groups?

I never did say that the government's policy was to provide a new house at once for every Canadian citizen. The Liberal government's policy is to provide adequate housing for everybody, and we are travelling just as rapidly as we can in that direction. I must remind my hon. friend of something he knows already, and that is that the act provides for subsidization. That is being applied, as the hon. member for Eglinton said today. There is an opportunity to make wider use of that provision but that is up to the municipalities and the provinces. The federal government stands ready to co-operate.
I think I have answered some of the questions raised by the hon. member for York West, who suggested a fixed rate of interest.

National Housing Act
I think that would be rather impracticable in a fluctuating money market. We have to compete for mortgage money, and we must set the interest rate at a value which will attract sufficient mortgage funds to the market.
The hon. member put considerable stock in equity in a house, just as I do. I believe his thinking is much the same as mine, and that is reflected in the act. We try to keep the down payment as low as possible, having in mind on the other hand the need for equity in the house and bearing in mind also that the lowest possible down payment is not always the greatest service that can be rendered to a borrower, because it simply means that he is being saddled with higher carrying charges. That is one of the biggest obstacles that can be placed in the way of a greater level of house building for those who need houses. The problem of land assembly which he mentioned is a very real one, and we have been giving a lot of consideration to it.
The hon. member for Yukon cited the problem that obtains in that northern country. I am able to give him some encouragement by telling him that we are looking at it by way of studying the regulations to see to what extent they can and should be changed to meet the conditions he mentioned.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond raised a problem which seems to be a little more acute in his particular constituency but which nevertheless prevails right across Canada; that is, the need to build housing on adequately serviced property. I know the particular problem which confronts him in the low lying areas of Sea island, Lulu island and other places in that constituency. We had the problem up about a year ago and with his help and co-operation were able to move forward by allocating available building approvals to builders in the area. I am sure that in the same spirit of co-operation between him and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the builders we will be able to continue the high level of building there.
The hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort spoke about the use of the limited dividend section of the act in Saskatchewan. I must say that this is one province in which good use has been made of that section. The provincial government has asked that the provisions be broadened to provide for a certain amount of hostel accommodation, and that has been done. The only difference is in the matter of degree. The Saskatchewan government asked Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to provide for one hostel unit for each self-contained unit in a limited dividend project. The matter was given a great deal of consideration and the board of

Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has now made a proposal which I consider reasonable. That is they will provide a maximum of one hostel unit for every two self-contained units in a limited dividend project.
I think there was some question in the minds of the Saskatchewan government about the cut-off date. We had set June 30, I think it was, but we informed the Saskatchewan government of that date last August so it seems to me they have had considerable opportunity to be appraised of the ruling laid down by the board of the corporation and adjust themselves to it.
That concludes my remarks. There are a number of points of details which I think could be taken up with advantage when the various clauses of the bill are being considered.

Mr. Chairman, there are some brief remarks that I should like to make on points raised by the minister in his reply.
First of all I should like to say a word about the interest rate and the recent increase in it. I point out that the increase in the interest rate is directly attributable to the policy laid down by the central bank and imposed by it upon the chartered banks. This is not at all a case of the effective rate under the act automatically adjusting itself in the ordinary course of the play and interplay of economic forces, adjusting itself to supply and demand; this is purely and simply a case of an increase in the rate being brought about by the action of the Bank of Canada.
Therefore it seems to me that here we have a fundamental contradiction in government policies. The minister has declared the desire of the government to see the house construction rate maintained and if possible built up to a further record this year, but the fact remains that another branch of government, the central bank, then the chartered banks in turn and now the government itself in connection with the interest rate on these loans, have increased the rate. This is all the result of government action. I still say that there is here a contradiction in government policy.
In referring to the Regent Park North project and the Regent Park South project in Toronto the minister made no comment upon a circumstance which it seems to me is of considerable importance. In the Regent Park North project there was no requirement as to minimum income of tenants, but in connection with the proposed Regent Park South project Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation proposes that there shall be required a minimum income of $150 a month

for every tenant. As I tried to say this afternoon, that seems to run counter to any concept of the provision of housing accommodation to meet a need.
It seems as though the aim of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in establishing that minimum requirement is to prevent any financial loss. They are concerned about making the project pay its way. I had thought that a higher consideration here was the meeting of need of families whose need of housing accommodation of this kind is well established. How the government justifies the imposition of that minimum requirement in relation to income on those who hope to qualify as tenants in the Regent Park South project I have yet to learn.
Next the minister sought to establish by assertion that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has sought public participation and interest on the part of citizen groups. I can only say to him that whether or not that has been the avowed purpose of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation officials, the fact is that they have created on the part of citizen organizations which played a leading part in bringing about and sustaining the success of the Regent Park North project the impression that their interest is neither sought nor wanted by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
I think, in view of what the minister has said, it is not unreasonable to ask the officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to take more concerted measures to show their desire to have participation on the part of these interested civic organizations, because there cannot be any question at all about their intelligent interest in these projects, and it is altogether desirable that there should be understanding and co-operation between them and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
I was surprised at the minister's remarks about the degree of consultation and cooperation that he says exists between the housebuilders and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. That remark did indeed surprise me, because I have in my hand a press clipping from the Globe and Mail of September 27, 1955, in which we find the following:
Charges were levelled last night at a meeting of the 600-member Toronto metropolitan home builders' association that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation was:
Adding $500 to $1,000 to the price of each new house by imposing and enforcing a growing list of regulations governing construction;
Appointing inspectors to inspect inspectors, and alleging infractions of regulations where infractions did not exist;
Handicapping contractors by arbitrarily and unfairly holding back advance payments on mortgage money;
National Housing Act
Attenpting to drive the small builder out of business.
"They are making us put Cadillac trimmings on Ford products," said Louis Rice, chairman of the association's C.M.H.C. liaison committee.
Then we read further:
Over the past year, C.M.H.C. rules and regulations have added $500 to $1,000 to the price of each house.
I am well aware that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation officials, when these charges were made public, undertook to make a denial the following day. But when the minister says that there is close co-operation between the two, I think it is only correct that this information should be brought before the house, because it does not sound t<* me, in the face of those charges, even taking account of the denial that followed on the part of C.M.H.C. officials, as though there is any great degree of co-operation disclosed, at least in that press report.

Let me say a word on that. That clipping I believe, speaking from memory, arose out of the remarks of only a few delegates to that convention. I do not think a resolution ever came forward. It had to do with the inspection standards. There were some who felt the inspection standards of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation were too rigid. The officials of Central Mortgage went to the meeting the next day and said they would be delighted to have discussions on all the points. I believe it was the general consensus of the meeting, even before the officials of Central Mortgage got there, that the position of Central Mortgage was one that should be defended rather than criticized.

As I have said, I was well
aware the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation did not admit these charges were justified. Indeed, there was a denial of them. I simply come back to the minister's assertion of co-operation existing between housebuilders and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
It does.

Well, it must exist in other
quarters within the body mentioned, namely the metropolitan home builders association, than those of its members whose comments were noted in that particular press report.
This is my final comment. The minister has not touched on the point that was raised earlier, that is, the fact that those who are able to qualify for mortgage loans under part I of the housing act are to an increasing degree those of substantially above-average incomes. It may be that as the act is at present constituted some of this is inevitable, but at any rate it seems to me the

National Housing Act
point ought to have the attention of the government and is worthy of comment on the part of the minister.
Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has not attempted to deny this. As a matter of fact one of its publications in this respect attracted some comment, for in it appeared an indication that the immediate effect of the amendments in 1954 to the National Housing Act was to:
-enable potential borrowers in the higher family income ranges to obtain more expensive houses for a smaller cash outlay.
Then I read further in the quotation the following:
The average gross family income which includes the total income of all dependents of a loan applicant in addition to his own income, was $5,477 under the new act in 1954 compared to $4,961 under the old act in 1953.
Under the new act, 53 per cent of these borrowers had gross family incomes of $5,000 or more, compared to 37-7 per cent in 1953.
Borrowers in the family income group of under $4,000 represented 15-5 per cent of the total under the new act compared to 25-4 per cent under the old act in 1953.
So the evidence is undeniable-indeed it is readily conceded by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation-that in the past few years, whether it is the result of the new amendments or the result of other factors that would have made themselves felt whether there had been amendments in 1954 or not, the benefits under part I of the act have been moving more and more in the direction of higher income families, and the proportion of families in the income levels below $4,000 who are deriving benefit under part 1 of the act is constantly shrinking.
It seems to me that this is a fact that cannot be viewed without a degree of concern bordering on alarm. This is not to suggest that these benefits should be withdrawn from those in the group earning $5,000 and over, but I think it calls for some concerted examination of the fact that these benefits are not accruing, under the present provisions of the act and the administration, to those whose incomes are less than average.

There may be some very competent men there who are capable of continuing on such a board from year to year. From my own experience I would say it is altogether desirable that there should be some of the elected representatives in the city council sitting on such a board. My own experience in that respect, when I sat for three years as the representative of the Toronto city council on the city planning board, convinced me that liaison of that kind is altogether desirable. Often there are some very competent officials who have a great deal of knowledge and experience, and f think that knowledge and experience can be put to very good use when these persons are permitted to serve on the boards of limited dividend housing corporations set up under municipal auspices.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue) moved
subtopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND DENMARK FOR THE AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 8, to implement an agreement between Canada and the Kingdom of Denmark for the avoidance of double taxation with respect to income tax.
He said: Mr. Speaker, you will note that this is a bill to implement an agreement between Canada and the kingdom of Denmark for the avoidance of double taxation with respect to income tax. I draw that to your attention because of the fact that previous

agreements with other countries also included succession duties. Succession duties are not a part of this agreement.
The purpose of the bill is to give legal effect in Canada to the agreement which, as a result of negotiations and subsequent exchanges, has been reached between the government of Canada and the government of Denmark for the avoidance of double taxation and the establishment of rules for reciprocal fiscal assistance in the matter of income taxes, which agreement was signed at Ottawa on the 30th day of September, 1955. The provisions of the agreement are similar in their effect to those contained in the agreements which Canada has made with the United States, the United Kingdom, Sweden, New Zealand, France and Ireland. It is designed to avoid double taxation and also provides for the exchange of information.
By means of an exchange of reciprocal tax credits the country of residence gives credit for the tax imposed by the country in which the income has its source. As in the other agreements, taxation by a state of the trading profits of an enterprise of the other state is limited to those attributable to the (permanent establishment of such enterprise in the first mentioned state. In addition, certain specific provisions are made regarding the profits from the operation of ships and aircraft, and the exemption from tax of exchange teachers and students.
I suggest the important part of the bill has to do with the schedule, and when we get into committee and come to the discussion of the schedule I shall be very happy to give such explanation as may be required in answer to any questions that may be asked.

Question
The following answer, deposited with the Clerk of the house, is printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:

1.	What percentage of the cost of the St. Lawrence seaway will be borne by the United States?
2.	Is the Canadian or the American government giving any consideration to an eastern entrance to the St. Lawrence seaway?
3.	Is either the Canadian or American government giving any consideration to the construction of the Chignecto canal as an eastern entrance to the St. Lawrence seaway?
4.	Has the government discussed the matter of the Chignecto canal with the United States in its relationship to the St. Lawrence seaway?
Answer by: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of
Slate for External Affairs):
1.	Most recent estimates of expenditure on both the power and navigation aspects of the St. Lawrence seaway indicate that the United States will bear 43-4 per cent of the total cost of the project. It is estimated that the
United States will bear 30-2 per cent of the navigation project and 50 per cent of the power project. This calculation does not include the sums expended by either country on existing works, such as the expenditure by Canada on the Welland canal.
2.	The eastern entrance to the seaway is considered to be the point where dredging begins in the St. Lawrence river to permit navigation. The Canadian government is not giving consideration to changing this definition nor, as far as we are aware, is the United States government.
3.	The Canadian government is not giving consideration to the construction of the Chignecto canal as an eastern entrance to the St. Lawrence seaway. We have not been informed of any consideration given this matter by the United States government, but such consideration is unlikely as any canal through the Chignecto isthmus would be wholly in Canadian territory.
4.	The Canadian government has not discussed with the United States authorities the matter of the proposed Chignecto canal in relation to the St. Lawrence seaway.
